Trick or Treat? These Halloween Hazards Can Be Hellish For Dogs

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Dogster is reader-supported. When you buy via links on our site, we may earn a commission at no cost to you. Read about privacy.

It has been revealed that halloween packs a steady stream of costumed strangers and bowls of candy into a single evening, and for dogs that combination carries more hazards than most people expect. Most of the risks are easy to avoid with a little planning, and several of them start well before the first trick-or-treater arrives at the door. These precautions help keep dogs out of trouble while the rest of the household enjoys Halloween.

Halloween candy can be dangerous for dogs, and the wrappers create an additional hazard. Certain ingredients in sweets, including chocolate and xylitol, can be toxic to dogs, while swallowed wrappers can cause choking or digestive problems.

Keeping candy in a closed container at home is a good starting point, but the risk doesn't end at the front door. Keeping a close eye on what a dog sniffs or picks up can help prevent an unwanted snack from turning into a veterinary emergency.

Costumes for dogs can be adorable and hilarious, but only if the dog agrees. Not every dog feels happy playing dress-up, so itâs crucial to pay attention to how they respond.

Industry observers note that A costume should fit comfortably without restricting movement or creating opportunities for the dog to become tangled. An outfit that fit last year may now be too tight, while one bought for a puppy to grow into could be awkward or unsafe in the meantime.

Before heading out or welcoming visitors, check that the costume fits properly and your pup can walk comfortably in it.

Sources indicate that A Halloween costume can look adorable on a dog, but wearing one safely requires supervision. Some dogs become fascinated by their outfits and start chewing at loose fabric or accessories, potentially creating a choking hazard.

There's no reason every dog has to avoid costumes, provided the outfit is comfortable and the dog tolerates wearing it. But if the dog needs to be left alone, take the costume off. It's a simple precaution that reduces the chance of an otherwise harmless outfit causing trouble.

Halloween can be overwhelming for dogs that struggle with noise, unfamiliar people, or constant activity. Trick-or-treaters arrive throughout the evening, and costumes can make even familiar surroundings feel different.

Sources indicate that A dog that becomes overexcited or anxious may benefit from having somewhere quiet to retreat. A separate room with a comfortable bed, fresh water, and familiar toys can provide a welcome break from the commotion.

Make sure visitors understand that the dog shouldn't be disturbed if it chooses to settle somewhere away from the activity.

According to recent reports, jack-o'-lanterns, lights, and other Halloween decorations can make a home feel festive, but curious dogs may see them as things to investigate or chew. Keep decorations out of reach, particularly anything that could be harmful if swallowed.

Sources indicate that real candles inside pumpkins also pose a risk if a dog knocks one over. Battery-operated alternatives are a safer choice, especially in areas where pets can wander freely.

Glow sticks and glowing bracelets help make children more visible during evening trick-or-treating, but their bright colors and flexible shapes can also attract a dog's attention.

The liquid inside can cause irritation and may be harmful if swallowed. A dog that bites through a glow stick could end up ingesting the contents, so these items should be kept well away from curious mouths.

According to recent reports, check the ground during walks, too, particularly on Halloween night when discarded glow sticks and bracelets may be lying around. If a dog chews or swallows one, contact a vet for advice.

Handing out candy can mean opening the front door dozens of times in a single evening. For a dog that's curious, excitable, or easily frightened, those repeated opportunities can make an escape more likely.

Closing the door between visitors helps prevent a dog from slipping outside unnoticed. Another option is to step outside to greet trick-or-treaters and close the door behind you.

Sources indicate that keeping the dog in a separate room during busy periods adds another layer of protection. It also reduces the chance of a dog becoming startled by costumed visitors appearing at the entrance.

An identification tag and microchip are always a good idea, but they become particularly key on a night when doors are opening frequently, and unusual sights may startle a dog.

If a dog escapes, an ID tag with current contact details gives whoever finds it a straightforward way to get in touch. A microchip provides another means of identifying the dog and helping it return home.

It has been revealed that check that the dog's tag is attached securely and that the contact information associated with its microchip is up to date. These small steps can make a significant difference if a dog gets loose.

Halloween can be stressful and dangerous for dogs, but it doesnât have to be. Keeping candy secured, choosing comfortable costumes, providing a quiet retreat, and making sure the front door stays closed can prevent many of the problems associated with the holiday.

It's also worth remembering that dogs may react unpredictably to unfamiliar costumes and unusual activity, even if they're normally relaxed around visitors. Staying attentive from the first doorbell to the last helps keep the evening enjoyable for everyone, including the four-legged members of the household.

It has been revealed that maybe it is having a family that loves them. Maybe it is a warm bed, a full bowl, and a safe place to sleep. Or maybe luck is something a little more fundamental: having people who see you as an individual and take the time to understand what you need.

At Lucky Dog Rescue and Adoption Center near Lake Chapala, Mexico, the dogs may still be waiting for permanent homes, but in the meantime, they are surrounded by caring people who show up for them day after day.

At Lucky Dog, everyone has a unique way to help and collaborate.

Recent findings suggest that some volunteers walk dogs. Others train them, clean their enclosures, help with fundraising, or coordinate veterinary care. Some foster dogs in their homes. Others help with the less visible work that keeps the center running.

In a recent development, when I visited Lucky Dog, I arrived with Mark and Nancy. Mark helped build the Thursday volunteer group, bringing together people who wanted to help in different ways.

âI've gotten to know a lot of people who want to help, and somehow Thursday became our day. We have our group, and everybody has something they can do. You don't have to do everything. You just have to show up and help with what you can.â.

It has been revealed that mark has an injured knee, and at the moment, he cannot walk the long distances over cobblestone roads around the center, but he and Nancy have their own crucial role. They bring chairs into the enclosures and spend about 20 minutes with the dogs, offering pats, treats, kind words, and ear scratches. The dogs happily settle in beside them.

According to recent reports, different volunteer groups cover each day of the week. Some take dogs for walks, while others help with training, cleaning, maintenance, administration, or fundraising.

That Thursday, each person simply did what they came to do. For the dogs, every part of that effort is what makes them feel lucky.

During the day, the dogs stay in pairs in larger enclosures. They are taken out for long walks or playtime in the larger garden areas around the center. In the mornings and evenings, Valentin, one of only two paid workers at the rescue, moves the dogs between their daytime and nighttime enclosures and feeds them breakfast and dinner. During the day, volunteers help with walks, playtime, training, and puppy lunchtime.

At night, the dogs return to smaller individual enclosures.

When a dog needs medical attention, a veterinarian comes to the center to examine and treat them. Volunteers then follow the veterinarian's instructions and continue treatment.

From Valentin's morning and evening routine to the volunteers who walk, train, feed, and care for the dogs, many people contribute to a Lucky Dog's day.

Industry observers note that the roots of today's Lucky Dog Rescue go back to 2001, when Geoffrey Kaye and Lourdes Avila started an animal shelter in Riberas del Pilar. When the shelter closed in 2012, the commitment to helping the area's dogs continued. Volunteers regrouped with veterinarian Dr. Antonio Ladron, and in December 2012, Lucky Dog Rescue and Adoption opened its doors.

Since then, the center has continued caring for abandoned and abused dogs while helping prepare them for permanent homes.

In a recent development, in 2025, Lucky Dog took in 23 dogs and placed 23 through adoption or transfer. Approximately 35 newly introduced volunteers joined, with around 30 committing to weekly shifts. The center's intended capacity is 22 dogs, yet its average monthly census was close to 30 during the year.

Those numbers give you some idea of the work happening behind every individual dog.

Spicy is dog-reactive and needs to be housed separately from other dogs. Mark has developed a close relationship with her, and she has a very clear opinion about where his attention should go.

âSpicy loves me, and she is not happy when she sees me go into a different enclosure to pet another dog,â Mark mentioned. âI have to do it in a way that I hide from her so she canât see or she won't stop barking.â.

It is a sweet story, but it also shows why understanding each dog's personality matters.

In a recent development, hope Procops, who works as a groundskeeper and guard at Lucky Dog, understands how key volunteers are to organizations like this. Itâs not just about the day-to-day tasks. Itâs about looking after the dogs in their care and preparing them for life beyond the shelter. She states the goal of Lucky Dog Rescue is âto ensure all the dogs in our care are kept healthy, loved, socialized, and given the best chance to find their forever homes.â.

Recent findings suggest that camille Short is in charge of training volunteers and dogs at Lucky Dog. Her approach goes beyond teaching basic commands. The goal is to help dogs develop skills that can help them succeed in a home.

According to recent reports, three young siblings, Sasha, Stephanie, and Sergio, were already showing how swiftly puppies can learn. They knew how to sit and lie down on command, and were learning to walk with their harnesses. They were highly motivated by treats and, judging by the puppy kisses, equally enthusiastic about people.

Two of the puppies, Stephanie and Sergio, have already been chosen by families; their adoption papers are signed and ready. Sasha remains available for adoption.

Sources indicate that as for Spicy, she arrived at Lucky Dog in 2022 and has been waiting for her fresh home ever since. Initially anxious and mistrustful, she has come a long way with the daily attention and interactions she receives from volunteers. Now, Spicy is looking for a confident new best friend.

Industry observers note that âEverything nice with a little bit of spice,â indicates Camille of Spicy. âShe loves people and attention but is selective about her four-legged friends.â.

Industry observers note that some dogs find their people swiftly. Others need more time, medical care, or someone who understands their particular personality. Until then, their days continue with walks, play, veterinary care, clean enclosures, treats, kind words, and volunteers who take the time to understand them.

Vice President of Lucky Dog Rescue, Darryl Painter, describes the mission as:.

âImproving animal welfare in Lake Chapala via rescue, adoption, community, and fostering.â.

The sense of community was tangible during my visit, but perhaps what stayed with me most was how much we humans and dogs have in common. We are all sentient beings, and in our own ways, we all need to be acknowledged, accepted for who we are, and given the opportunity to love and be loved.

In a recent development, at Lucky Dog, those needs are met in many different ways. A walk, a clean enclosure, a treat, a kind word, or simply having someone take the time to know an individual dog.

Maybe that is what makes them lucky.

Not just having people who care for them, but having people who take the time to know them.

It has been revealed that and that is something anyone can do. Whether it is volunteering, fostering, sponsoring, or simply offering time and attention, there is a way to help.

And every morning, people arrive.

Someone opens an enclosure.Someone picks up a leash.Someone brings a treat.

And perhapsâ¦that is what makes these dogs lucky.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that hydrangeas really have their moment during the summer months, and then spend the winter looking dead, brown, and crispy while we politely look away. Shea McGee, however, has made a point of doing the opposite, and to beautiful effect!

According to recent reports, that's right, folks; not only did the Netflix Dream Home Makeover star give her hydrangeas some attention in winter, but she also added them to the star of the show during the holidays: her Christmas tree! And, much like Sarah Jessica Parker's floral Christmas tree, it's one of those oh-so-simple but oh-so-effective ideas that we can't believe we didn't think of first.

Industry observers note that as you may or may not know, Shea grows Limelight hydrangeas at her Salt Lake City home, telling fans that the blooms “bring me so much joy in the summer”. Is it any wonder, then, that when the interior designer shared a video of her Christmas decor to Instagram, the blooms were front and center?

In a recent development, A post shared by McGee & Co. (@mcgeeandco).

As you can see above, Shea McGee has decorated her tree with warm brown, tan, and cream ornaments, dried orange slices, clip-on LED candlesticks, and dried hydrangeas from her own garden (although you can buy ready-to-go cone hydrangeas from McGee & Co if you prefer an easier life).

It's a beyond brilliant idea, as it means the blooms get a second act, which is a better return than most shrubs give you. If you want a similar look, just read on for some tips from the experts.

Shop Shea McGee-Inspired Christmas Decor:.

It has been revealed that keen to give it a whirl from scratch? Look this way...

Cameron of DreamHowYouLive favors Limelight (the same as Shea McGee grows) and Annabelle for a hydrangea arrangement. “Their petals dry stiff and papery, so they keep their shape, where softer mopheads crumble.”.

In a recent development, flower farmer-florist Joey McFarland of Flowers by Dr. Jo agrees that panicle types like Limelight are best for long stems. He warns that bigleaf hydrangeas set buds in fall, so cutting too deeply means “cutting off your blooms for next year.” Shopping for plants? Browse our list of panicle hydrangea varieties.

Sources indicate that timing is highly important as well, especially when it comes to hydrangeas. Morgan Brooks of Plant Style Home waits until the heads “turn papery and antique in early fall.” Cut too soon and, as Cameron warns, “they wilt instead of drying.” (Which means you need to show patience, grasshopper).

According to recent reports, when it comes to drying hydrangeas the experts all have a different opinion, which tells you how difficult it can actually be. Floral preservation artist Nadi Melam of Florals Memories says, “I always dry hydrangeas in a vase of water,” about an inch, for a “lovely muted antique color.”.

Cameron hangs them upside down in a dark, dry spot for two or three weeks, since vase-dried heads “tend to droop.” Our guide to drying hydrangea flowers covers both.

According to recent reports, the best rule to follow if you want the Shea McGee effect? Water-drying holds shape and color well, while air-drying is quicker but leaves blooms more fragile.

Recent findings suggest that there’s one place where most people go wrong when drying hydrangeas for Shea McGee-style decor. As Cameron tells me me he cuts the head town to 3-inch stems, wires each branch and tucks the whole bloom into a gap. His personal rule: “Three small clusters spread around the tree look intentional. It has been revealed that arslan Ali of DecoroDea advises, “Treat them like picks, not ornaments,” and says to place them last, “after the ornaments and lights are already on,” so you fill the gaps that are actually still dark. Brooks wires clusters low near the trunk first, then moves smaller heads toward the tips. In essence, you can take a bit from every expert tip.

For McGee’s look, add dried orange slices, cream and tan ornaments, and warm white lights. Bright white, Cameron notes, makes “the whole thing look cold.”.

Dried petals shed, which is why Melam is so blunt with their advice: “You lose petals every time you touch a flower.” Cameron’s fix is a light hairspray mist that “keeps the shedding down.” And, as for those annoying relatives, who “just want to adjust one thing,” tell them that your Shea McGee-inspired Christmas tree is now a museum exhibit, so hands off".

If you don't have real hydrangeas in your yard, faux hydrangeas as a no-mess alternative. These cream-white stems give the same soft look without the shedding.

Hydrangeas are also toxic if chewed, so keep clusters out of reach of curious pets.

Those candles on Shea McGee’s Christmas tree? Make them LED.

Melam claims, “Open flame is a no-no since the dry material will ignite right away.” As for saving them for next year, the experts are once again split.

Want a warm glow like MsGee's but without the fire risk? These warm white, dimmable clip-on LED candles come with a remote, so you can keep real flames far from your dried hydrangeas.

Recent findings suggest that melam stores heads flat in a box with tissue between layers, and Cameron has reused the same heads two years running. However, McFarland indicates dried blooms “won’t do particularly well in storage” and suggests composting them and cutting fresh ones.

A member of the gourd family (Cucurbitaceae), the pumpkin is a cultivated squash, technically a fruit, with both savory and sweet culinary applications. While some countries wouldnât dare serve a roast dinner without a generous helping beside their potatoes, in the US, the nutritious pumpkin is usually relegated to seasonal decorations or the key ingredient in the eponymous pie.

It has been revealed that there are more than 100 varieties of pumpkin with slightly different textures, flavors, and recipe applications. What they all have in common is that they are low in calories, high in antioxidants, rich in vitamins & minerals, and, when prepared correctly, safe for dogs to eat.

Recent findings suggest that compared with the potato, a vegetable commonly used in both human and canine recipes, the pumpkin is higher in fiber, much lower in carbohydrates, and is far more digestible. It is often included in diets for cats and dogs with digestive problems due to its beneficial impact on intestinal health and function.

Even the seeds of certain pumpkin varieties, when properly prepared, have been found to help eliminate intestinal parasites.1.

In a recent development, and the cherry atop this pumpkin pie? Most dogs find the taste of pumpkin irresistible.

Yes, pumpkin is a safe and healthy food we can share with dogs, but there are some dos, donâts, and precautions to be aware of.

Pumpkin is a delicious, healthy, and nutritious food that deserves to be seen as more than just a Halloween decoration or pie ingredient. Dogs love the taste, and their digestive systems will thank you.

#136235. What Your Snake Plant Needs in November – 5 Winter Care Checks to Keep It Glossy and Thriving

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1141 w)

General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Gardeningknowhow ↗ Open Full Page

What Your Snake Plant Needs in November – 5 Winter Care Checks to Keep It Glossy and Thriving

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1141 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gardeningknowhow

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Most of the year, a snake plant really is about as hard to kill as people say.
  • Good snake plant care in winter is mostly about doing less and getting the timing right.
  • Take a few minutes with your plant in front of you and work through five checks.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Most of the year, a snake plant really is about as hard to kill as people say. But that changes in November. The days get short, and the heat comes on, and the watering habit you kept all summer now leaves the potting mix wet for weeks. Yellow leaves and soft, mushy bases tend to follow.

Good snake plant care in winter is mostly about doing less and getting the timing right. Once light levels drop, your snake plant isn't growing much, so it uses far less water and needs no fertilizer at all. What it does need is a dry pot between drinks, steady room temperatures, and a spot out of the cold air that pools along windows.

Take a few minutes with your plant in front of you and work through five checks. Run through them now, then again on a gray afternoon in December. That alone considerably cuts the odds of losing a snake plant to winter.

Don't rely on a calendar when watering snake plants. A snake plant that needed water every two weeks in July might go a month or more between drinks in November. Its surface won't tell you much. So how do you know when it's dry? Push a finger down as far as it goes, or try the chopstick trick: push a wooden skewer to the bottom of the pot and pull it out. Damp mix clings to the wood and darkens it; dry mix leaves it clean.

According to recent reports, if you're struggling to know when to water, then use a moisture meter for an accurate assessment, like the Xlux instant read probe, available from Amazon. Water only when the whole depth comes up dry, then let the pot drain fully. Leaves that go soft or flop over at the soil line usually mean the roots have sat wet too long.

Low light is something a snake plant tolerates, not something it grows well in. In November, the sun sits lower and the days are short, so a dim corner that was fine in June may now get very little light. Growth slows, and the mix stays wet far longer because the plant is barely drawing water.

A spot within a few feet (about a meter) of an east or west window helps. Make the move gradual, though – a plant that goes straight from a dim hallway into hours of direct south sun can scorch.

Without a bright window, a grow light like the Sansi Pot-Clip-On Grow Light, positioned a foot or so (30 cm) above the leaves, fills the gap.

On a cold evening, hold the back of your hand near the window where your snake plant sits. Chilly on your skin means chilly on the leaves, too. Blame single-pane glass, the gap under an outside door, or a nearby heating vent. Any of them can swing the temperature more than a snake plant can take – even while the thermostat reads fine.

Industry observers note that ordinary room temperatures are what you're after, roughly 60–85°F (16–29°C). Trouble starts if the plant sits below about 50°F (10°C) for long stretches. Leaves pressed against cold glass can develop soft, water-soaked patches. So at night, pull the pot back a foot or two (30–60cm) from the window.

If you want to see what the plant goes through after dark, then use a high/low thermometer, like the TempPro digital indoor thermometer, which displays both high and low temperature and humidity levels.

According to recent reports, tip the pot and look underneath. Drainage holes get plugged with compacted mix, a stray pebble, or roots that have grown through. In a decorative cachepot, a snake plant can stand in an inch (2.5 cm) of old water without anyone noticing. Lift it out and check. If the mix is still wet a week or more after you watered, it may have broken down and is holding too much moisture.

Winter is a poor time to disturb roots, so repotting snake plants is normally a spring job. The exception is a pot that won't drain at all – or a mix that stays soggy no matter what. Then a careful repot now beats rotting roots in March. For a replacement, choose a pot with a drainage hole and its own saucer, like this Vigoro ceramic planter from Home Depot. Fill it with a gritty potting mix, like Miracle-Gro Cactus, Palm, and Citrus Mix, which drains much faster than regular potting soil.

Look each leaf over, down to the soil line, for signs of common snake plant problems. If yellow is creeping up from the base and the leaf feels soft or mushy there, you're looking at overwatering and rotting roots. Cold damage can look a lot like it, though. Wrinkled or curling leaves usually mean the reverse: the plant went too long between drinks.

Next, check the crevices where leaves overlap for pests. Cottony white tufts there are mealybugs (Planococcus citri), and small tan or brown bumps that stay put when nudged are scale (Coccus hesperidum).

In a recent development, dab a few with a cotton swab dipped in rubbing alcohol, then follow up with a ready-to-use insecticidal soap, like Garden Safe insecticidal soap, sprayed right onto the insects. It's far easier to deal with a dozen now than hundreds in February.

It has been revealed that put the fertilizer away until spring. A plant that isn't actively growing can't use the feed, so unused salts build up in the mix and can burn roots. Hold off on routine repotting for the same reason. Fresh mix and a bigger pot push a plant toward latest growth right when the light to support it is lowest. Disturbed roots also recover slowly in a cool room.

Don't water your snake plant on a schedule just because the heat is drying out the air. Dry air and dry soil aren't the same thing, and a snake plant copes with dry air far better than it does with wet roots. For the next few months, you want it holding steady, not growing.

Recent findings suggest that run the same five checks again around the fresh year. In winter, a snake plant mostly needs the right spot and to be left alone. Give it that, and the one looking a bit tired in November is usually putting up new leaves by late spring.

For years, business owners and property managers have wrestled with the same question: how do you tell the difference between a legitimate service animal and a pet that someone is trying to pass off as one?

Itâs a question John Bradford spent years trying to answer, first as a property manager overseeing thousands of rental units, and now as the founder of PetScreening, a platform used to verify animal accommodation requests across more than 7 million rental units nationwide.

With the rising number of service dogs and emotional support animals leading to incidents of confusion, conflict, and exploitation, John sets the record straight on how to verify a real service animal from one that isn't, and what you are legally allowed to ask.

The truth is that most people donât fully understand the laws around service animals and emotional support animals, and even well-meaning questions can come across as anything but. That gray area and confusion can create real risk. Ask the wrong question, and a business can face a discrimination complaint. Ask no questions at all, and policies and rules become easy to bend, which leads to potentially dangerous situations.

Getting this right protects everyone involved, including the people who genuinely rely on these animals every day.

Under the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA), service animals are defined as:.

âDogs that are individually trained to do work or perform tasks for people with disabilities.â.

Disabilities vary widely, from physical and sensory to psychiatric, intellectual, and neurological. The needs of each person are different, so the trained tasks may look different from person to person. The ADA cites that the service animal must be a dog or, in rare cases, a miniature horse. Federal law does not require certifications, registrations, vests, or ID cards for these animals.

Industry observers note that beyond the specification that the animal must be trained to perform tasks, the legal standard is limited, so it can be difficult to easily identify which animals are legitimately service dogs and which are not. This is where public confusion starts.

In a recent development, there are plenty of ways to make a dog look like a service animal, like labeled vests, âregistrationâ certifications, and IDs, but none of these are federally supported. A dog wearing a vest isnât automatically a service animal, and a dog without one isnât automatically a pet. What matters legally is not appearance or paperwork. Itâs the dogâs trained ability to perform certain tasks.

According to recent reports, this is the distinction many find hardest to grasp, and it matters because different laws apply to each. Service dogs are protected under the ADA and, due to their training and the tasks they perform, they are permitted in public spaces such as restaurants, retail stores, and hotels. That could mean guiding someone who is visually impaired, alerting an owner to an oncoming seizure, or reminding them to take medication. Service animals are also protected under the Fair Housing Act and require paperwork if the disability or need for the animal is not obviously understood.

In a recent development, emotional support animals (ESAs) are different. Their value comes from the comfort their presence provides. They donât necessarily have to be dogs, they arenât required to be trained to perform specific tasks, and theyâre not covered by the ADA to be allowed in public spaces like restaurants.

Recent findings suggest that they are, however, protected by the Fair Housing Act. Under this, landlords are generally required to make allowances for an ESA if a tenant has appropriate documentation from a licensed healthcare provider establishing a disability-related need. Examples of disabilities warranting an ESA include, but are not limited to, anxiety disorders or autism.

Sources indicate that ESA accommodations are supposed to come through legitimate means, typically an established relationship with a licensed medical or mental health professional who can document the need. But some people have found loopholes for this by filling out forms online or paying fees for instant letters, which only fuels public skepticism about the legitimate need for these animals. Not to mention, this abuse can make people wary of service dogs, too.

According to recent reports, while there is no foolproof visual test, trained service animals typically display consistent, recognizable behaviors. These dogs show exemplary discipline and obedience to the commands of their handler. They have the ability to ignore external distractions from other dogs, people, food, sounds, and smells while focusing on the needs of their handler. They display a calm temperament and are not aggressive or anxious. It is also expected that these animals be quiet, unless they are tasked with alerting an owner to a medical issue, and that they are housebroken and trained to walk on a leash without unnecessary pulling or circling.

Recent findings suggest that this is where business owners and landlords need to tread carefully. When it isnât obvious that a dog is a service animal, staff are permitted to ask:.

Is this dog required because of a disability?

What task has it been trained to perform?

According to recent reports, thatâs the full extent of it. Staff should not ask about the nature of a personâs disability, demand documentation or proof of training, or require dogs to demonstrate their tasks. Asking beyond the two questions, even if it comes from a place of genuine curiosity or caution, can expose a business to discrimination claims.

Industry observers note that news stories about supposed service animals harming bystanders in public continue to raise questions about the legitimacy of those animals, and businesses are often caught in the crossfire. These incidents are symptoms of a larger problem: businesses and property owners navigating without clear guidance, while people with legitimate needs are met with suspicion.

Service animals and emotional support animals play an essential role in the lives of the people who rely on them, and protecting that role starts with understanding the rules.

Sources indicate that if you own a business or manage a property, you donât need to become legal experts overnight, but you do need a consistent, fair process that respects peopleâs rights and keeps everyone safe. When everyone knows where the lines are, the people who truly depend on these animals can go about their lives without facing doubt at every door.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the holidays often leave us with more food than we know what to do with, don't they? Before throwing everything into the compost or bin, though, take a look at your Thanksgiving leftovers; your feathered friends could be very thankful for them!

Yes, some everyday ingredients from the feasting table can make welcome treats for backyard birds, offering a little extra nourishment as temperatures drop and the nights draw in (and transform your outdoor space into a welcoming bird sanctuary in the process).

Whether you're hoping to see your birth month bird out there, or just happy to offer your kitchen scraps up to any local critters who might make use of them, here's how to use your Thanksgiving leftovers to keep bird feeders filled over the holidays...

Before we dive on in, a word of caution: not every Thanksgiving dish is suitable for wildlife, especially as salt, butter, rich sauces and seasonings can make seemingly harmless scraps unsuitable for birds.

The trick? Try to save a few simple ingredients before they make their way into the casserole dish or onto the dinner table. With that caveat in place, then, here are seven Thanksgiving kitchen scraps worth keeping...

Sources indicate that have a few apples left over from your Thanksgiving preparations? Birds such as robins and other fruit-eating visitors will definitely appreciate small pieces of fresh apple.

In a recent development, cut the flesh into bite-sized chunks, removing the core and seeds first. Bruised apples are fine so long as they're fresh (they're not as fussy as we are!), but discard any mouldy or spoiled pieces. And avoid offering apple pie filling or cooked apples covered in sugar and spices.

Recent findings suggest that cranberries are a Thanksgiving staple, and you'd better believe that their fresh (and unseasoned, obviously) counterparts make a lovely treat for birds. Offer a few whole or chopped cranberries on a clean feeding tray like this one from MIXXIDEA.

Frozen cranberries are fine, too, once thawed. Just avoid cranberry sauce, as it typically contains added sugar and may include other ingredients birds don't need. Honestly, a little fresh fruit is all that's required.

Pecans (again, plain and unsalted) are another holiday favorite that can be shared with feathered visitors, along with walnuts and peanuts. All of these scrummy nuts are rife at Thanksgiving, and all provide fats and protein that can help birds maintain their energy during colder weather.

According to recent reports, take care to chop larger nuts into manageable pieces and check that they haven't been coated in salt, sugar, chocolate or seasoning. Just like the fruit, nuts should be fresh, too, rather than stale or musty.

Corn often features on the Thanksgiving menu in a big way, and a few plain kernels can be offered to garden birds; just set aside a small portion before adding butter, salt or other seasonings.

According to recent reports, cooked or fresh corn kernels can be placed on a feeding tray, but avoid creamed corn, buttery corn casserole and heavily seasoned dishes. Only offer a little at a time, as damp corn can spoil quickly.

If pumpkin or squash features in your holiday cooking (or your Thanksgiving decor, if you're Kristin Davis!), don't throw away all those seeds; instead, rinse away any stringy pulp, remove any seasoning and allow the seeds to dry thoroughly.

Sources indicate that offer them (have I gotten too repetitive yet?) plain and unsalted, either whole for larger birds or broken into smaller pieces for smaller visitors. They're a useful source of fats and nutrients, making them a worthwhile addition to your bird feeding station.

Leftover rice can also be shared with birds from your Thanksgiving feast, provided it hasn't been cooked with salt, butter, oil, garlic or onions. Both white and brown rice are suitable in small quantities when prepared plainly.

Industry observers note that P.S. There's a persistent myth that uncooked or cooked rice swells inside birds and causes harm, but this isn't true. Nevertheless, rice shouldn't replace more nutritious bird food, so just offer just a small amount (you may find your birth month winter bird adores it) and remove anything uneaten so it doesn't have a chance to go bad.

According to recent reports, A little leftover boiled or baked potato from your Thanksgiving prep can be another treat for your feathered friends. Set aside a portion before adding butter, milk, salt or gravy, then allow it to cool and chop it into small pieces.

In a recent development, please never offer raw potatoes or green potato peelings, and avoid chips, roast potatoes cooked in fat and heavily seasoned mashed potatoes. Experts always advise that plain potato be treated as an occasional extra rather than a regular food source.

It's every bit as important to know what to avoid when it comes to feeding birds your Thanksgiving leftovers. Turkey fat and pan drippings might seem like an easy substitute for bird suet, but they're best kept off the feeding station. Audubon, in fact, warns that turkey fat melts more readily than traditional suet and can turn rancid rapidly. It can also smear onto feathers, potentially affecting their waterproofing and insulation.

Industry observers note that gravy, stuffing and salty side dishes should also stay off the menu, as they often contain butter, salt, onion and garlic, none of which are suitable additions to a wild bird's diet. Avoid, too, anything that contains chocolate, along with avocado, sugary desserts and heavily processed foods, too. Bread and pastry aren't particularly nutritious (even if they won't do any harm), so think up some better ways to use your leftovers; might this author humbly submit the idea of a bread-and-butter pudding?

According to recent reports, once you've picked all of the bird-friendly scraps out of your Thanksgiving feast, be sure to present it properly! Always use a clean feeding tray rather than leaving piles of food on the ground, and try to put food out in the morning, as this is when it's most likely to be eaten.

In a recent development, take care to remove anything uneaten before it spoils, and wash feeding surfaces regularly to reduce the risk of bacteria and disease spreading. It's also worth keeping fresh drinking water available, particularly as colder weather approaches, and remember that kitchen scraps are supposed to be occasional extras, not a replacement for a balanced wild bird food mix.

Still, all those warnings aside, there's no denying that sharing a little of your holiday feast with your local birds is a lovely way to give thanks to Mother Nature (and reduce food waste at the same time).

In a recent development, my dog, Reggie, has Cherry eye. If left untreated, can it have a negative effect on his vision? Money is an issue for me right now.â.

According to recent reports, cherry eye happens when the gland of the third eyelid, which helps produce tears, slips out of its normal position and becomes visible as a pink or red cherry-looking bulge in the corner of your dog's eye. I understand that veterinary expenses can be difficult to manage, and it is crucial to know what needs attention right away and what can safely wait a bit longer.

Cherry eye does not usually cause blindness directly, but leaving it untreated can put Reggie's eye health at risk. The exposed gland can become irritated, inflamed, or damaged, and its tear production may be reduced over time. Because this gland contributes to keeping the eye moist and protected, reduced tear production can increase the risk of dry eye, a condition that can lead to corneal damage, scarring, and impaired vision if it becomes severe. Think of the gland as part of the eye's built-in lubrication system. Even if the eye looks comfortable today, problems can develop gradually.

If surgery is not financially possible right now, please arrange a veterinary examination to confirm the diagnosis, assess tear production, and check the cornea.

Talk to your vet about a payment blueprint, or you might be able to find a veterinary teaching hospital or nonprofit clinic that may offer lower-cost care. Your veterinarian may recommend a suitable lubricating eye product while you work toward surgery, but lubrication will not reposition the gland. Please make sure you avoid human eye drops, leftover medications, or steroid eye drops unless specifically prescribed, as some of these can worsen an undiagnosed corneal ulcer. The gland should generally be repositioned and preserved rather than removed. If the gland is removed, you would need to use eye drops to supplement Reggieâs tear production for the rest of his life.

In a recent development, please seek same-day veterinary care if you see Reggie squinting, holding the eye closed, rubbing it persistently, developing a cloudy or bluish cornea, or producing thick yellow or green discharge. These can be signs of a painful or more serious eye problem. If the eye is comfortable and clear, it may not be an immediate emergency, but I would not leave cherry eye unassessed for weeks or months. The most key first step is protecting the eye while finding an affordable treatment option.

The contest celebrates the behaviors that make dogs funny, unique, and truly memorable; the ones that make us smile when we think about them, while also highlighting  Embark's Behavior Insights & Training feature, which explores how canine DNA may influence behavior.

Sock Thieves, Bathtub Sleepers, and Other Household Oddballs.

Furry weirdos have interesting, different habits; Embark's examples include a dog who sleeps upside down in the bathtub, one who carries a sock around without chewing it, and a canine who spins exactly three times before lying down. Not two. Not four. Three.

Then there's the dog who refuses to walk past one particular house, or the dinner diva who won't touch a meal until someone has given it the full restaurant treatment.

Such behaviors are entertaining partly because they are so unique and specific. Most pet parents can share at least one story that would make a perfectly reasonable person wonder what goes on inside that furry little head.

A sock might be a very treasured object, a source of comfort, a reminder of their favorite personâs scent, or simply something fun to carry. A particular walking route might feel uncomfortable for reasons a person cannot detect, most likely a scentâ¦ but then again, who knows? And a bedtime ritual may have started with nothing more mysterious than finding a comfortable position.

It has been revealed that of course, some dogs are just little weirdos, and that's part of their charm. But there's a difference between a pup who has always slept with their legs in the air and one who suddenly starts acting strangely. If your pup begins staring at walls, repeating the same movements, or turning down food when that's not normal for them, don't automatically label it as a new amusing personality trait. Pain, illness, and anxiety can all show up as changes in behavior. If something feels off, put the camera down and call the vet.

Industry observers note that genes can influence behavioral tendencies, but they don't write a complete script for an individual dog's life. Learning and environment play a massive role, too, sometimes in ways pet parents never intended.

Recent findings suggest that take the sock thief. A dog grabs a sock, their pet parents react with dramatic excitement, and suddenly the household is involved in a thrilling chase. From our perspective, it's a laundry crime. From the pup's perspective, it may be an excellent fresh game.

Sources indicate that behaviors that lead to positive or rewarding outcomes are more likely to happen again. Attention, play, food, and access to preferred activities can all reinforce behavior, even when nobody is training anything on purpose.

Genetics can contribute, too. Inherited tendencies may influence a dog's motivation to chase, retrieve, explore, or seek food. But a predisposition doesn't guarantee a particular behavior, nor does it explain every individual habit. A dog's behavior comes from a combination of biology and learned experience, which is often less convenient than blaming everything on their breed, but it is much closer to reality.

A 2022 study published in Science looked at the behavior and DNA of thousands of dogs. Researchers found that a dog's breed explained only about 9% of the differences in behavior between individual dogs. In other words, dogs of the same breed can have very different personalities and behaviors. Genetics plays a role, but it doesn't tell the whole story.

In a recent development, that doesn't mean genetics is irrelevant. The researchers found evidence that many behavioral traits do have a heritable component. Rather, the findings show why breed alone is a poor crystal ball for predicting how an individual dog will behave.

Some dogs may be especially motivated to retrieve, chase, or investigate, reflecting tendencies shaped partly by their ancestry and breeding history. But individual dogs still vary, and experience helps shape how those tendencies appear. However, with more data, we may learn latest things; science is ever evolving along with our technologies.

Embark's Behavior Insights & Training feature connects genetic information with behavioral insights and training guidance. Genetic results can be useful, but they are one piece of the puzzle and not a personality prediction.

Behavior is best understood in context. Has the habit been present for years, or did it start last week? What happens before the behavior? Could pain, fear, stress, or another medical concern be contributing?

If a pup is safe and comfortable, there's often no reason to stop a peculiar routine unless itâs a problem. A dog who carries a favorite toy around the house doesn't need a corrective training proposal. When a behavior does create a problem, redirection and positive reinforcement can help teach an alternative response without relying on intimidation or punishment. This is the science of behavioral modification.

The goal isn't to turn every pup into a perfectly polished obedience champion, but to help us understand what each dog needs and help them become great family members.

Your Compost Pile Needs These 6 Things Before Winter If You Want to Make Black Gold Through the Cold

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that did you know that your compost pile keeps working over winter?
  • Industry observers note that during winter composting, microorganisms slow down their activities, and freezing temperatures can temporarily stop them, but they won’t necessarily die.
  • Tackle these six tasks now to keep composting at home this winter.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that did you know that your compost pile keeps working over winter? While the decomposition process might slow, microorganisms are still active in compost as long as it doesn’t freeze. Ignoring your compost over winter is a missed opportunity to keep making and using the garden's black gold.

Industry observers note that during winter composting, microorganisms slow down their activities, and freezing temperatures can temporarily stop them, but they won’t necessarily die. A sufficiently large and well-managed compost pile can stay warm enough in the center to keep the little critters working and breaking down waste materials.

Tackle these six tasks now to keep composting at home this winter. Even if decomposition slows in the cold, these steps will help you get more usable compost earlier next spring. Our tips work for all main types of composting, including open heaps, compost bins, and enclosed tumblers.

Sources indicate that now is a good time to remove any finished compost to use as winter mulch in your garden beds. Then, it’s time for one last turn for the season. Turning compost helps aerate the pile, introducing oxygen to the microorganisms that need it to decompose materials. It also distributes moisture and materials more evenly.

A sturdy garden fork will do the job, but a compost aerator tool, like this Squeeze Master one from Amazon, makes it much easier to get air deep into the pile without having to dig everything out and turn it by hand.

This should be your final turn before freezing conditions begin. You don’t want to keep turning compost over the winter, as this will release heat and slow the decomposition process. As you make the final turn, look for and break up any wet clumps or large pieces of material that haven’t broken down much. If you note a sour or rotten smell, add more dry, brown materials.

In a recent development, larger compost piles retain heat better than smaller piles because they have a greater volume of material relative to their surface area, which is exposed to the cold. The more you can add to your pile now, the more likely it is that the center will remain warm and active throughout winter. A long-probe compost thermometer, like the Vivosun Compost, is a handy way to check what's happening deep inside the pile without disturbing it.

It has been revealed that for a compost pile, aim for three feet (0.9 m) wide, deep, and high. Bulk up your pile during your final turn, adding a good mix of green and brown materials. Be sure to add enough dry, coarse material to absorb moisture. A large pile won’t be any good if it becomes waterlogged and so compacted that there is no airflow.

While you don’t want to turn your compost again this winter, you can still add layers of waste to it as the season progresses. Green materials, like kitchen scraps, keep coming all winter, but brown materials tend to be harder to come by. Browns include dry leaves and twigs as well as cardboard, untreated paper, and straw.

Sources indicate that good compost should have layers of each type of material, so stockpile your harder-to-find browns now. As you add kitchen scraps over the winter, layer in some of these stockpiled brown materials to maintain a good balance. A countertop compost caddy, like the Oxo Good Grips Easy-Clean Compost Bin, makes it easy to collect kitchen waste indoors until you're ready to take it outside. Keep a bin or pile of leaves and twigs from fall yard waste, as well as shredded paper and cardboard.

It has been revealed that A large pile with extra waste material will help insulate the active center of your compost pile, but you can also take extra steps to insulate and protect it from cold winter temperatures. This will slow heat loss. It’s important that you take insulating steps before the compost pile freezes.

One easy way to insulate the pile is to surround it on all sides with straw bales or bags of leaves. If you don't have straw on hand, you can pick up full-sized straw bales from Tractor Supply to create a protective barrier around your compost pile. You can also add a layer of straw or leaves on top. Wood chips and finished compost are also efficient insulators.

If you have a bin or tumbler, another option is to surround it with insulating materials. Just be sure you still have easy access to add materials throughout winter.

Sources indicate that winter precipitation can saturate a compost pile, causing it to become compacted and reducing airflow. Moisture can also wash away the valuable nutrients you’re trying to collect. If you have an open compost pile, cover it with a tarp that will allow precipitation to run off and away from the compost. A heavy-duty Everbilt tarp from Home Depot is a durable option that you can secure in place to keep winter rain and snow out. If you have a bin, keep a lid on it.

Recent findings suggest that while keeping moisture out is important, compost still needs airflow in winter. Don’t completely seal your pile with protective coverings. If you have a bin with a cover, there should be drainage and air holes. Make sure these don’t get clogged.

Moisture balance is always important in compost. It’s important to check and adjust this balance before your compost freezes this winter. To optimize microorganism activity, the composting material should feel damp when you squeeze it in your hand without excess moisture running out of it.

Industry observers note that if your compost feels too wet, incorporate more dry, brown material. If the pile is too dry, you can add a little water before there is a real danger of it freezing. Throughout winter, as long as temperatures allow it, continue to check the pile for moisture balance and adjust as needed.

According to recent reports, many gardeners might wonder: are these efforts worthwhile, or does compost just shut down for winter? Compost does continue to break down in winter, sometimes with temporary stops during freezing conditions.

However, it’s crucial to have realistic expectations. While microorganisms continue to break down compostable materials in winter, their processes do slow down significantly. Larger, insulated piles are more likely to stay active and break down faster than smaller piles or compost in uninsulated bins. Taking these steps to keep your pile warmer in winter is worth the effort if you can keep microorganisms active and working.

Sources indicate that it’s important to note that if you practice vermicomposting, you should provide extra protection for the worms over winter. To keep it active over winter, keep your vermicompost bin indoors where you can control the temperature.

Winter doesn't have to put composting on hold. A little preparation in autumn can protect valuable organic material, reduce household waste, and give you a head start on producing nutrient-rich compost for the next growing season.

Sources indicate that for dogs that love burrowing, a bed covered in sheets and blankets can feel like an invitation to play. Digging, wriggling underneath the covers, and pushing through folds of fabric can all become part of the fun.

Bedtime can also signal that the day is winding down and an opportunity for cuddling is approaching. A dog that enjoys being close to its owner may become excited at the prospect of spending that time together.

Recent findings suggest that if playful behavior consistently earns attention, a dog may be encouraged to repeat it. Recent findings suggest that A dog that is still eager to run, jump, and play may need more activity before the household turns in for the night. An evening walk or a game of tug-of-war can help provide an opportunity to burn off some energy before bedtime.

A dog that's had enough exercise and stimulation is more likely to be ready to relax, rather than treating the mattress as a playground.

Many owners enjoy sleeping alongside their dogs, while others prefer to keep their beds pet-free. Sharing a bed can feel cozy and comforting, and having a dog nearby may also be soothing for people who experience anxiety or other mental health challenges.

Recent findings suggest that there are practical considerations, too. Dogs can carry dirt, bacteria, and parasites into the bed, and some owners would rather not have fur on their sheets or pillows.

Ultimately, whether a dog is allowed to sleep on the bed comes down to what works for the household. If itâs not a problem, then itâs not a problem. There's no single right choice, and a dog can still enjoy plenty of affection and companionship without sharing the mattress.

A dog getting frisky on the bed is often responding to a combination of familiar scents, opportunities for attention, and the chance to play somewhere comfortable. Blankets can add to the appeal, especially for dogs that enjoy burrowing.

For many dogs, the bed is simply an exciting place to be close to their favorite person. With a little preparation, bedtime can still end in a peaceful night's sleep rather than an impromptu wrestling match.

James Thomas Ashbacher, 37, of Spring Lake, North Carolina, a former U.S. government contractor, was arrested by the FBI on Tuesday for allegedly leaking national defense information by posting the information on a popular social media site, unlawfully retaining other national defense information at his residence, and stealing night vision goggles from the U.S. Army’s Special Operations Command.

Ashbacher was charged by an indictment unsealed Tuesday with unlawfully transmitting and retaining national defense information and with theft of government property.

It has been revealed that according to the indictment, beginning in or about 2021, the defendant worked as an employee of a private firm that provided security and emergency management services at the U.S. Army Special Operations Command facility in Fort Bragg, North Carolina. To perform the required functions of his employment, Ashbacher held a Top Secret security clearance with Sensitive Compartmented Information (SCI) access.

As further detailed in the indictment, Ashbacher photographed and removed without authorization videos and photographs containing images of classified military operations and transmitted the materials to a social media site. The classified materials were later re-posted by other users to a second social media site. Ashbacher asked a social media user in a private message to remove some materials and further stated that he was “trying to do some damage control.” A search of Ashbacher’s residence also revealed a classified award write-up that contained additional national defense information, along with a night vision goggle system specific to a military unit within Army Special Operations Command that had been reported missing.

The FBI Charlotte Field Office is investigating the case with substantial assistance from the U.S. Department of the Army’s Criminal Investigative Division.

Sources indicate that trial Attorney Leslie Esbrook of the National Security Division’s Counterintelligence and Export Control Section and Assistant U.S. Attorney Logan Liles for the Eastern District of North Carolina are prosecuting the case.

Abraham Teklu Lemma, 53, of Maryland, a former information technology contractor at the National Reconnaissance Office, the U.S. Department of State, and the U.S. Department of Justice pleaded guilty today to conspiring to commit espionage on behalf of the government of the Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia.

Lemma pleaded guilty to conspiracy to transmit national defense information to a foreign government and has agreed to be incarcerated for a period of between 120 and 262 months.

Sources indicate that “Lemma betrayed the United States to an extraordinary degree,” noted Assistant Attorney General for National Security John A. Eisenberg. “He exploited his IT administrator access to remove classified national defense information, including Top Secret information, from a secure facility and transmitted it to Ethiopian government officials hoping they would use it to target and kill paramilitary fighters in a regional conflict. Clearance holders pledge undivided loyalty to the United States and bear a legal and moral responsibility to protect classified information. Those who betray this trust will be prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law.”.

Industry observers note that “For more than two years, Lemma exploited a position of trust to provide highly classified U.S. government information to a foreign government,” said U.S. Attorney Jeanine Ferris Pirro for the District of Columbia. “In doing so, he betrayed his oath, his colleagues, and his country, while jeopardizing our national security. His guilty plea sends a clear message: those who compromise America’s most sensitive secrets will be investigated, prosecuted, and held accountable.”.

According to recent reports, “Despite swearing an oath to defend the Constitution of the United States, Abraham Lemma betrayed our country by committing espionage on behalf of the Ethiopian government,” said Assistant Director Roman Rozhavsky of the FBI’s Counterintelligence and Espionage Division. “By his own admission, Lemma provided classified national defense information to Ethiopian officials, who then used it in military operations during an ongoing conflict. This guilty plea should serve notice that the FBI and our partners will work tirelessly to stop foreign intelligence services, and anyone who decides to work with them, against the interests of the United States.”.

Sources indicate that “Today’s guilty plea makes clear that any attempt to betray the United States, violate the trust of the American people, and compromise our national security will not be tolerated,” remarked Assistant Director in Charge Darren B. Cox of the FBI Washington Field Office. “Lemma abused his position of trust and access to some of our nation’s most highly classified information, conspiring with foreign government officials to unlawfully disclose materials protected to the highest level. In doing so, he not only endangered our national security but also betrayed the trust placed in him by the American people.”.

According to court documents, Lemma held a Top Secret U.S. security clearance. From 2021 until his arrest in August 2023, Lemma conspired with senior Ethiopian government officials to collect and transmit dozens of highly classified documents, notes, materials, and photographs, classified up to the Top Secret/Sensitive Compartmented Information (TS/SCI) level, to Ethiopian government officials. Material identified as “Top Secret” means that unauthorized disclosure of the material is reasonably to cause “exceptionally grave damage to the national security” of the United States.

Much of the highly classified information Lemma shared with the Ethiopian government concerned an armed conflict in Ethiopia. Lemma’s conspirators included senior officials within political, military, and intelligence branches of the Ethiopian government.

Industry observers note that during his espionage activities, Lemma took numerous steps to conceal his conduct. and surreptitiously removed classified documents and information from U.S. government holdings.

It has been revealed that specifically, Lemma wrote notes by hand with classified information and then hand-carried those notes out of secure U.S. government facilities. Additionally, as an IT administrator, Lemma removed electronic versions of classified information from classified U.S. government repositories and then removed the same classified information from secure U.S. government facilities where he worked.

According to recent reports, on some occasions, Lemma encouraged his Ethiopian government conspirators to take direct action against paramilitary groups who were fighting the government of Ethiopia. For example, on Dec. 18, 2021, Lemma told one conspirator, “We have to finish these people once and for all, otherwise there will never be peace in Ethiopia.” Later that day, Lemma shared additional information with his conspirator and wrote, “Please send Dro[nes].”.

In a recent development, according to the plea agreement, Lemma agreed to plead guilty to conspiracy to transmit national defense information to a foreign government. If accepted by the court, Lemma has agreed to be incarcerated for a period of between 120 and 262 months. Sentencing is set for April 14, 2027.

The FBI Washington Field Office investigated the case, with assistance from the U.S. Department of State's Diplomatic Security Service.

Industry observers note that the matter is being prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorneys Tejpal Chawla and Adam P. Barry for the District of Columbia, and Trial Attorney Kathryn DeMarco of the Department of Justice’s National Security Division.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that A Christmas tree might be the star of the living room in December, but once the holidays are over, it usually gets packed away or recycled. Festive houseplants, on the other hand? Well, they can stick around for years – and some might become so beloved that you can't imagine your home without them.

Whether you're looking to make your Christmas décor a little more lasting, or simply a self-confessed crazy plant lady in need of more houseplants (I'm right there with you!), then you should absolutely consider choosing a living plant this year.

From spectacular seasonal blooms to fragrant herbs and miniature trees, these five festive favorites offer plenty of reasons to keep growing long after the last present has been unwrapped.

I'm a huge fan of Christmas cactus, having inherited one that lived for an incredible 27 years before recently dying. (RIP, Noel; we barely knew ye!) It was a reminder of just how long these festive houseplants can last, and how attached we can become to them over time.

Industry observers note that christmas cactus (Schlumbergera) produces beautiful flowers in shades of pink, red, purple and white, usually just in time for the holidays. Even when it's not in bloom, though, its arching stems make an attractive display, particularly in a hanging pot.

Give it bright indirect light, keep it away from harsh sunshine and don't let its roots sit in soggy compost (mine loved life on our bathroom windowsill), and remember: a cooler spell and shorter days in fall help encourage flowering.

Few festive houseplants make quite as dramatic a statement as amaryllis (Hippeastrum). Its tall stems and oversized trumpet-shaped flowers bring a splash of color indoors when much of the garden is dormant, making it a favorite for Christmas displays.

Somehow, I have managed to keep my own diva alive for several years now (it's sitting on my desk as I type this, in fact), so I urge you not to discard the bulb once flowering finishes. Instead, remove the faded flowers, keep the leaves growing, give it light, water and occasional feeding as it grows, then follow a suitable resting period to encourage another round of blooms. With a little patience, the same bulb can reward you with flowers for many seasons.

You can pick up a bag of Amaryllis bulbs easily enough from the Garden State Bulb Store, if you fancy giving it a go; they'd make excellent holiday presents once you've gotten them started!

Sources indicate that if you'd prefer something compact and relatively easy to care for, Flaming Katy (Kalanchoe blossfeldiana) is a solid choice. This succulent produces clusters of bright flowers in red, pink, orange, yellow or white, and it's widely available during the festive season.

Its fleshy leaves store water, so it doesn't need constant watering (making it ideal for even the most forgetful plant parents everywhere). All you have to do is place it somewhere bright, allow the compost to dry a little between drinks, and avoid leaving it sitting in water.

Blooming in the fall and winter, what could be prettier than this Flaming Katy at Christmas?

Flaming Katy can be encouraged to flower again by providing a steady stint of uninterrupted nights in autumn, making it a holiday plant that's well worth keeping after its first colorful display.

Sources indicate that rosemary is a lovely way to bring fragrance into the home over the holidays, especially when sold clipped into a miniature living Christmas tree shape. Its evergreen needles look festive, while its scent adds a little something extra to the season – and you can snip sprigs for cooking, too.

I have actually kept my own rosemary going for a long time, bringing it in and out of the house with the seasons until it grew so large that it eventually had to move permanently into the garden. It just goes to show that a small festive plant can have quite a future ahead of it!

Industry observers note that rosemary (even one like this Rosemary Christmas Tree from the Three Organization Store) needs plenty of light and well-drained compost. Don't overwater it, and remember that it generally prefers cooler and brighter conditions than a hot room right next to a radiator.

For something a little different, why not choose a small tree? Fig, olive and citrus trees can all make beautiful container plants, bringing Mediterranean charm to a bright home.

A fig tree offers attractive foliage and the possibility of homegrown fruit, while an olive tree has silvery-green leaves and a timeless look. And there's no denying that a calamondin or miniature orange tree is particularly festive, with glossy foliage, fragrant flowers and colorful fruit that can linger on the branches.

In a recent development, naturally, these trees need the brightest spot you can offer, and citrus in particular appreciates warmth and consistent care. Indoor conditions aren't always ideal year-round, so check each tree's needs and consider moving it outdoors during suitable warmer months.

Recent findings suggest that A living Christmas plant is a gift that doesn't have to end when the festivities do. Choose yourself, then, a festive houseplant that suits your space, give it the care it needs, and you could be enjoying your festive favorite for many Christmases to come.

According to recent reports, or, you know, you could ask Santa to bring you one. Either or...

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Sources indicate that the catch is that only certain bulbs produce enough heat to help, and most modern porch strands won't help at all.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that every November, boxes of holiday lights come down from the attic, and a few gardeners start eyeing those tangled strands for a second job. On paper, Christmas lights frost protection sounds like a neighbor's tip over coffee – string up a potted lemon tree, plug it in, and hope it makes it to morning.

Industry observers note that there's some truth to it. Gardeners have relied on heat from old-style bulbs for years, and it can work alongside the usual steps for winterizing container plants, like covering pots or moving them under shelter. When used safely with a suitable cover or enclosure, that heat can nudge the temperature around a plant up a few degrees.

Sources indicate that the catch is that only certain bulbs produce enough heat to help, and most modern porch strands won't help at all. But using the right bulbs comes with its own risks. Mix hot bulbs, fabric covers, and unprotected electrical connections outdoors carelessly, and you have a fire and shock hazard.

Christmas lights keep plants warm only if the bulbs run hot. Old-fashioned incandescent bulbs, like these C7 Christmas lights from Amazon, give off a fair amount of heat along with their light, so running a strand beneath a properly supported frost cover or inside a cold frame can warm the small area around a plant. University of California Agriculture and Natural Resources advises home citrus growers to use traditional non-LED lights to provide extra warmth, with or without a frost blanket.

Colorado State University Extension measured the effect in cold frame trials in Fort Collins. One string of 25 mid-size C7 bulbs hung inside a covered cold frame, with a space blanket over the frame, kept each frame noticeably warmer than the night outside. A string also beat a single large bulb at warming the cold corners.

If you want to recreate an enclosed space like that, use a cold frame or mini greenhouse, but only if the structure allows the lights to be safely suspended away from the plants and covering.

Industry observers note that pick up a string of Christmas lights in a store today, and you'll likely find they're LEDs. They convert far more of their electricity into light, leaving little heat behind – fine for decoration but useless for shielding a citrus tree on a 28°F (-2°C) night. When it comes to LED lights, frost protection just isn't on the table – they don't generate enough warmth.

University frost guidelines specifically recommend incandescent bulbs when you need real heat. Traditional incandescent mini lights can provide some warmth, while larger C7 and C9 bulbs, like these from Novelty Lights Store, produce more heat per bulb.

Recent findings suggest that any set used should carry an outdoor rating and be suitable for the intended setup. With incandescent Christmas lights, plants under a properly supported cover can gain extra heat, but the same heat makes the bulbs a hazard if they touch foliage or covering materials.

Industry observers note that several vulnerable container plants could benefit, but growers most often protect potted citrus this way. Cold damage can begin around 30°F (-1°C), depending on the variety and duration of exposure, with limes generally more sensitive than mandarins. A potted lemon on the patio faces a specific risk that an in-ground tree doesn't. Its roots are far less cold-hardy than its branches, and the small amount of potting mix around them can cool and freeze much faster than the soil around an in-ground tree.

That means the lights can help through brief cold spells – just a few nights with light frost. They're not enough to protect tropical plants during weeks of hard freezes. A larger container holds more potting mix and can provide some extra insulation for the roots, so a pot like the ModernNest fiberstone planter from Walmart, designed to withstand freezing conditions, gives a citrus tree a sturdier home but won't prevent its roots from freezing.

In a recent development, hot incandescent bulbs can cause damage if they come into contact with foliage or covering materials. Incandescent bulbs can burn leaves if they touch them directly. Frost cloth, sheets, plastic wrap, and space blankets should never be pressed against the lights, where they can scorch, melt, or become a fire risk. Hang the strand so each bulb has enough clearance from surrounding materials, and use a separate frame, stakes, or supports to keep covers up and away from the bulbs. Make sure the lights are securely positioned so they cannot shift into contact with the covering.

According to recent reports, water and electricity can create hazards on cold nights. Use only outdoor-rated lights and cords outside, and plug them into a GFCI-protected outlet. Throw out any strand with cracked sockets or frayed wire instead of hanging it. Keep indoor strands and household power strips indoors, and don't rely on tape to waterproof electrical connections. Follow the manufacturer's limits on how many strings can be connected end to end, and follow the safety instructions packed with the product.

It has been revealed that start by moving the pot. An unheated garage, shed, or closed-in porch that stays above freezing can carry a citrus tree through a cold snap with no wiring. Pots that stay outside belong together, up against a house wall or in a corner out of the wind. Water them well before the cold comes, since moist potting mix freezes more slowly than dry.

Sources indicate that covers and wraps add another layer. Lowe's sells a 2-ounce frost blanket that can go over the plant on cold nights and come off during the day. Around the container, slip on an Eonox drawstring pot insulation cover to keep cold wind off the root zone.

For plants that need steady heat for weeks, a thermostatically controlled heater inside a greenhouse built to house one is the safer setup – the Dr Infrared greenhouse heater has an adjustable thermostat.

Recent findings suggest that under a cover or in a cold frame, old incandescent holiday lights can add a few degrees, maybe enough to see potted citrus through a short, light frost. You can't count on them, though, and the method needs careful setup, even though it's recommended by several university extension services. An LED strand won't give a cold plant any real protection.

Using hot bulbs with fabric and outdoor power for improvised heating carries risks that are easy to underestimate. Proper shelter, insulation, and a good frost blanket are generally safer options, although they won't always provide as much warmth as a safely heated enclosure.

Industry observers note that for most gardeners, the simplest solution is to keep the twinkling lights on the porch this year and move your lemon tree into a frost-free garage when cold weather hits. It'll still be green when the holiday decorations go back in the attic.

According to recent reports, tyler’s passion began with indoor gardening and deepened as he studied plant-fungi interactions in controlled settings. With a microbiology background focused on fungi, he’s spent over a decade solving tough and intricate gardening problems. After spinal injuries and brain surgery, Tyler’s approach to gardening changed. It became less about the hobby and more about recovery and adapting to physical limits. His growing success highlights that disability doesn’t have to stop you from your goals.
