Second Amendment Roundup, I: The Common Use Test and the Federal "Assault Weapon" Ban

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (793 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Reason

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Connecticut argues before the Supreme Court, in its Grant v.
  • That argument exhibits a profoundly mistaken view about the what the federal law actually did.
  • First, while the law made it "unlawful for a person to manufacture, transfer, or possess a semiautomatic assault weapon," that provision did "not apply to the possession or transfer of any semiautomatic assault weapon otherwise lawfully possessed under Federal law on the date of the enactment of this subsection."  18 U.S.C.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Connecticut argues before the Supreme Court, in its Grant v. Higgins brief, that before 2004, "few civilians owned AR-15s." That was supposedly "because federal law prohibited 'manufacture, transfer, or possess[ion]' of the weapons between 1994 and 2004" under Pub. L. No. 103-322, 108 Stat. 1796, 1996-97 (1994). That was the federal "assault weapon ban" that expired in 2004. The brief continues, "Under the common-use-only approach, if Congress had extended that legislation in 2004, AR-15s would never have entered into common use—and thus could be banned today.".

That argument exhibits a profoundly mistaken view about the what the federal law actually did.

First, while the law made it "unlawful for a person to manufacture, transfer, or possess a semiautomatic assault weapon," that provision did "not apply to the possession or transfer of any semiautomatic assault weapon otherwise lawfully possessed under Federal law on the date of the enactment of this subsection."  18 U.S.C. § 922(v). So it did not ban possession or transfer of a single firearm that was already lawfully possessed. Moreover, the federal law did not ban future manufacture of the subject firearms as long as certain aspects were eliminated. The firearms were defined, first, in a list of names, including "Colt AR-15" and "copies or duplicates" thereof. Second, they included certain features, including:.

a semiautomatic rifle that has an ability to accept a detachable magazine and has at least 2 of –.

(i) a folding or telescoping stock;.

(ii) a pistol grip that protrudes conspicuously beneath the action of the weapon;.

(iv) a flash suppressor or threaded barrel designed to accommodate a flash suppressor; and.

(v) a grenade launcher…. 18 U.S.C. § 921(a)(30).

It has been revealed that under the above, Colt could not engrave simply "AR-15" on its rifles, but could use other names. A manufacturer could not make a "copy or duplicate" of an AR-15, but as discussed below, a rifle would be a "copy or duplicate" of an AR-15, inter alia, only if it had at least two of the five listed features.

Industry observers note that but guess what: the sine qua non of an AR-15 is the conspicuously protruding pistol grip. None of the other features listed above are inherent in the AR-15 design. Many AR-15s never had a folding or telescoping stock. How many people cared whether it had a bayonet mount? A flash suppressor (or threading "designed" to accommodate one) could not be mounted, but a muzzle brake or compensator could. Congress must have included grenade launcher to sound dramatic, as that was already restricted under the National Firearms Act.

It has been revealed that and so the federal law did exactly nothing to "ban" the basic AR-15 design. Manufacturers kept making and consumers kept buying semiautomatic rifles with protruding pistol grips sans bayonet mounts.

Recent findings suggest that manufacturers submitted samples of rifles to the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF) to verify compliance. I have reproduced some samples of ATF approval letters in my Firearms Law Deskbook § 10:6 (available in book form or on Westlaw). As an example, ATF examined a Bushmaster XM-15E2, which was "based on the AR15 design and incorporates a pistol grip that extends conspicuously beneath the action of the weapon." However, it had none of the other listed features. It did have a muzzle brake, but it was not a flash suppressor. The rifle was found not to be an assault weapon "because it does not have at least two of the features specified in the statute. Additionally, the firearm is not a copy or duplicate of the Colt AR15 rifle." Edward M. Owen, Jr., Chief, ATF Firearms Technology Branch, Feb. 16, 1996.

Instead of a two-feature test like the expired federal law, Connecticut bans rifles based on a single feature, including: "Any grip of the weapon, including a pistol grip, a thumbhole stock, or any other stock, the use of which would allow an individual to grip the weapon, resulting in any finger on the trigger hand in addition to the trigger finger being directly below any portion of the action of the weapon when firing…." This is a more capacious ban that affects a much broader collection of firearms than the expired federal law.

Connecticut is wrong to argue that had Congress extended its law in 2004, "AR-15s would never have entered into common use—and thus could be banned today." AR-15s were already in common use in 1994. The fact is that the federal law did nothing to dampen the ever-increasing demand for and use by the American people of the AR-15 basic design. And it goes without saying that semiautomatic rifles with detachable magazines had already been around for a century when the federal law was in place.

Dan Roberts for Family Handyman.

“For a minor scorch mark on a laminate countertop, skip the abrasive cleaner. Buff it out with car wax or a mixture of toothpaste and baking soda instead.” —ELAINE WHITFIELD.

Industry observers note that “Build a simple dispenser for your trash bags using 1/2-in. pipe and a few fittings. To find a selection of the best countertop water filters for home use, we began by evaluating dozens of popular models, focusing on ease of installation and use, filtration claims, capacity, and price.

According to recent reports, after selecting seven units for testing, we performed the same set of steps with each, starting with installation. Next, we performed water quality tests before and after filtration to measure contaminant reduction, followed by blind taste tests to rate flavor and odor. We measured flow rate by timing how long each unit took to process or dispense a quart of water, assessed how easy each unit was to clean and change filters on, and rated general convenience of extra features like filter life indicators and removable pitchers.

We used each model for a minimum of 2 days to get a feel for how much we liked them overall, and for the faucet-connected models, to see whether they got in the way during regular tasks like washing hands or dishes.

The best countertop water filtration system for your home will depend on the quality concerns you want to address, how much filtered water your household uses, and how much daily upkeep you’re willing to take on. It’s smart to request a copy of your local utility’s Consumer Confidence Report or use a home water test kit, then compare potential systems’ filtration claims, capacity, footprint, and replacement-filter cost.

In a recent development, countertop water filters generally fall into two broad categories: reservoir-based systems and faucet-connected systems. Reservoir models don’t connect to your plumbing at all, while faucet-connected models attach to a standard faucet or use a diverter valve under your sink.

Industry observers note that reservoir systems hold untreated water in one tank or chamber and deliver clean water into another after it passes through the system’s filter(s). The simplest versions are water pitchers like the Epic Water Filters Pure XP Water Filter Pitcher or gravity systems like the Big Berkey Gravity-Fed Water Filter. Since they don’t connect to your faucet, they’re great for apartments, dorms, RVs, and kitchens with incompatible faucets.

Countertop reverse osmosis systems also use a refillable reservoir, but rather than relying on gravity, they have an internal pump that forces the water through their filters before delivering it to a pitcher or your glass. RO systems have the added benefit of reducing dissolved solids in untreated water, but that includes beneficial minerals like calcium and magnesium and also creates wastewater that must be dumped (or used for things like cleaning or watering plants).

Faucet-connected filters either attach directly to your faucet or connect via a hose and diverter valve. When the diverter is switched to the filtration setting, tap water filters through the unit on demand and into your glass, bottle, or pot. When the diverter is off, water flows straight out of the tap as normal.

In a recent development, two major things to consider regarding faucet-connected systems are faucet compatibility and installation. Most aren’t compatible with pull-down, pull-out, spray, sensor-operated, or nonstandard faucets, and many also have small hoses that connect the faucet to the machine, which takes up a bit of space and can look cluttered. Some allow you to run the hoses from the machine to the plumbing under your sink, but that will require an adapter and a hole in the counter for the cords to route through.

While it can be tempting to choose the purification system for water that has the longest list of contaminants removed, it’s ultimately more vital to pair the system you choose with what you’re actually trying to filter out of your water.

Recent findings suggest that most of the best water filters have activated-carbon filters that remove unpleasant tastes and odors and may reduce other chemicals or particulates. Some systems add sediment filtration or specialty media to target things like lead, fluoride, or PFAS compounds. Since performance varies by model, always check the manufacturer’s claims rather than assuming they all work the same.

Reverse-osmosis systems use a membrane designed to reduce dissolved solids, which means they generally remove more contaminants than basic filtration systems. However, they can also reduce beneficial minerals, which is why some manufacturers are now adding a remineralization stage to return the filtered water to a more alkaline state.

According to recent reports, many of the units on this list carry third-party certification to verify tested performance beyond manufacturer claims. NSF International’s drinking-water treatment standards are the most commonly used, although you may also see mentions of accredited organizations like IAPMO R&T or WQA. While our tests using the Varify Complete Drinking Water Test Kit for this guide backed up the manufacturers’ claims, it’s still a good idea to prioritize products that carry filter certifications and look up which contaminants the product is certified to remove.

According to recent reports, then, match the certification to your specific concern. For example, if lead reduction is your main goal, you’ll want a model with NSF 53 and 58 listings.

Capacity has two meanings: how much water a filter can treat before replacement and how much filtered water the unit can provide at once. For our purposes, we’re defining it as how much it can filter at once, as we discuss filter life in the next section.

Sources indicate that since reservoir models’ ready-to-drink supply is based on the size of their clean-water chambers, larger households or those with greater needs will want to prioritize a model that holds multiple liters or gallons. Faucet-connected models can also be a good choice in those situations, as they can deliver clean water continuously as long as the tap is on.

In a recent development, flow rate—how promptly the filter provides clean drinking water—is another important consideration. However, many manufacturers don’t list this information, and it can also vary depending on water pressure, source-water quality, temperature, and cartridge age. If this is a major concern, you may want to reach out to manufacturers directly or read online reviews for mentions of filtration speed.

It has been revealed that every countertop drinking water filter system requires filter replacement on a set schedule, which means the true cost of ownership ends up being more than what you paid for it. When choosing between systems, compare the number of filters, their individual projected filter capacity, and each one’s replacement cost.

A basic pitcher may use a single cartridge that’s easy to change but needs more frequent replacement, while a multistage RO unit may have multiple filters that each have different change intervals and prices. While systems with filter-life indicators can make it much easier to know when it’s time to swap them, if your unit is noticeably slower or isn’t providing the same quality, you may still need to change filters even if it isn’t technically time.

Countertop water filters are generally pretty straightforward, but the following answers to commonly asked questions can answer any lingering queries you may have.

According to recent reports, water filters work by using a filtration mechanism to capture organisms and chemicals that lead to unsafe or cloudy water. A fabricated surface traps the larger contaminants, while a compound like activated carbon works as a magnet to trap smaller contaminants.

Installation depends on the type: A faucet-connected filtration system typically attaches to a compatible faucet aerator or diverter valve, while dispenser, pitcher, gravity-fed, and countertop RO models generally only require rinsing the parts, installing the filters, and filling the reservoir. Always follow the manufacturer’s instructions, especially for RO units that may also require an initial flush cycle.

No, countertop water purification filters do not work with every type of kitchen faucet. Specifically, more modern designs and detachable faucets with spray nozzles may be incompatible with faucet-connected countertop water filters.

Most filters can remove chlorine, fluoride, bacteria, and parasites. To know exactly which contaminants a specific filter can remove or reduce, consult the manufacturer’s information regarding filter certification.

Yes, bacteria can grow in a countertop filter, so it’s a good idea to flush the faucet for about 20 seconds after turning on the water and then for an additional 5 to 10 seconds to filter and flush out any bacteria that may be lingering in the faucet.

Sources indicate that yes, countertop reverse osmosis systems are worth it for households seeking to remove dissolved contaminants like lead and fluoride and who prefer a plumbing-free setup. However, they generally cost more and require more maintenance than pitchers or carbon-filter-only units, so they’re best when your water test or local report identifies concerns simpler filters can’t address.

Filter replacement timing varies by system and filter type, so it’s best to follow the manufacturer’s schedule for your specific system. Generally speaking, pitcher and faucet units may need newly introduced filters every few months, while countertop RO filters and membranes may last anywhere from 6 months to 2 years. You may need to replace filters sooner if the flow slows noticeably or your water develops an unusual taste or odor.

  • Navigating a new parking lot can be confusing and stressful.
  • Recent findings suggest that parking lot designers think about how vehicles enter spaces, where drivers back out, and how much room cars need between rows.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Family Handyman's Editorial Process.

Angled parking spaces aren't just a design choice. Their layout can make turning easier, control traffic, and change how a lot uses space.

Navigating a new parking lot can be confusing and stressful. Some have one-way traffic, some have different parking rules. Even the parking spaces themselves can vary, with some lots using straight spaces and others using diagonal parking spaces. It turns out that small difference is intentional.

Recent findings suggest that parking lot designers think about how vehicles enter spaces, where drivers back out, and how much room cars need between rows. Learn why some parking lots use diagonal spaces, how the layout affects traffic, and what drivers should watch for.

Sources indicate that diagonal parking spaces are easier to pull into because drivers don’t have to make as sharp a turn. This is especially helpful in busy lots where cars are frequently coming and going. These spaces usually face one-way lanes, allowing drivers to pull in from the same direction. This helps keep traffic moving and reduces the chance of cars approaching each other head-on.

In a recent development, drivers still need to follow the arrows, though. Entering from the wrong direction makes it harder to pull into a space and can put drivers in the path of cars backing out.

Not always. According to the Iowa Statewide Urban Design and Specifications, “One-way angled parking provides fewer spaces than perpendicular for the same length of aisle.”.

In a recent development, the benefit is that one-way angled parking allows for narrower driving lanes, since drivers don’t need as much room to turn. Two-way angled parking is also possible, though Iowa’s guidelines say it’s generally less efficient than other layouts.

In a recent development, there’s also a downside to consider. Backing out of an angled space can be difficult when neighboring cars block the view, especially larger trucks and SUVs.

In a recent development, some streets use back-in angled parking to address this problem. Drivers back into a space so they can pull forward when leaving. According to the University of Kentucky, Kentucky Transportation Center, “With the front of their vehicle facing the street, a motorist has improved sight distance when leaving a parking space.”.

According to recent reports, back-in parking also lets passengers get out toward the sidewalk and keeps loading and unloading away from traffic. For regular diagonal spaces, drivers should back out slowly and watch for approaching cars and pedestrians. Backup cameras can help, but they shouldn’t replace checking the surrounding area.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, in Viramontes and Grant, Cook County and Connecticut argue that 19th century restrictions on Bowie knives provide historical analogues under Bruen for banning what they call "assault weapons."  They further contend that the widespread use of Bowie knives disproves application of the Heller test that arms in common use are protected by the Second Amendment.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, in Viramontes and Grant, Cook County and Connecticut argue that 19th century restrictions on Bowie knives provide historical analogues under Bruen for banning what they call "assault weapons."  They further contend that the widespread use of Bowie knives disproves application of the Heller test that arms in common use are protected by the Second Amendment. If Bowie knives in common use by law-abiding citizens may be banned, the argument goes, so too may semiautomatic rifles.

A word of caution. To paraphrase Freud, sometimes a knife is just a knife. Knives generally have a point and an edge on one side, sometimes also an edge on the other. Any knife can be used for good or bad. Bruen distinguished heavy weapons of war like lancegays from daggers, noting that in medieval society "[a]lmost everyone carried a knife or a dagger in his belt," "[c]ivilians wore them for self-protection," and "the smaller medieval weapons … strike us as most analogous to modern handguns.".

No doubt Bowie knives were in use as tools for skinning game and self-defense, and ruffians are remarked to have carried them concealed. But for a variety of reasons, it's unnecessary to decide whether Bowie knives met the Heller test of being in common use. Four of the amicus briefs are right on point on this issue: National Rifle Ass'n (NRA), National Shooting Sports Foundation (NSSF), Senator Ted Cruz, and the United States (U.S.).

First, a few States' restrictions are not enough to establish a historical tradition. Under Heller, a handful of outlier laws cannot justify a ban. "Most States regulated Bowie knives in some manner, but, except in a few outlier jurisdictions, adults were free to buy, possess, and openly carry them. Regulations typically restricted concealed carry, sales to minors, or imposed enhanced penalties for criminal misuse." NRA Br. 5.

According to recent reports, second, "No State banned Bowie-knife possession in the nineteenth century." NRA Br. 36. "And one of the only laws that likely did actually ban Bowie knives (along with pistols and an array of other items) is the same 1837 Georgia law that was promptly held unconstitutional other than as applied to concealed carry—because it was too restrictive to comply with the Second Amendment. See 1837 Ga. Acts 90, §1 (1838); Nunn v. State, 1 Ga. 243 (1846); cf. Bruen, 597 U.S. at 54 (singling out Nunn as "particularly instructive" on the Second Amendment's meaning)." NSSF Br. 21.

Sources indicate that these were concealed-carry restrictions, not complete bans. "This Court has already concluded that restrictions on concealed carry cannot justify carry bans, see Bruen, 597 U.S. at 48-49, 53-55, let alone possession bans, see Heller, 554 U.S. at 628-29." NSSF Br. 21.

Industry observers note that third, the same laws covered handguns. "If those laws justified rifle bans, then handgun bans would be justified all the more, because they typically also regulated handguns but not long guns." NRA Br. 38.

Industry observers note that where Bowie-knife restrictions were upheld, courts applied the same standard Petitioners advance here: arms in common use for lawful purposes are protected, while weapons used only by criminals are not. As Judge Richardson's dissent in Bianchi explains, it does not matter that courts sometimes disagreed about whether Bowie knives were in fact in common use, because they were applying the same yardstick. "State courts have long applied the common-use test to judge such laws under state constitutional provisions securing the right to bear arms." U.S. Br. 12.

Fourth, even a court that viewed the Bowie knife as exceptionally deadly held that the right to carry it was protected. "And Texas's Cockrum v. State held a Bowie knife to be a protected arm—"[t]he right to carry a bowie-knife for lawful defense is secured, and must be admitted"— while sustaining an enhanced penalty for its abuse, treating the weapon's dangerousness as a reason to regulate its misuse, not a reason to deny that it was an arm. 24 Tex. 394, 402-403 (1859). Cockrum is the mirror image of the decision below: alleged dangerousness bore on regulation, not on coverage." Cruz Br. 18.

The historical answer to misuse was punishing criminals, not disarming law-abiding citizens.

"[T]he evil must be prevented by the penitentiary and gallows, and not by a general deprivation of a constitutional privilege." U.S. Br. 30 (quoting Wilson v. State).

7 Surfaces You Should Never Use Ice Melt On

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Avoid damaging salt-sensitive outdoor surfaces with these expert-backed suggestions.
  • Recent findings suggest that ice melt salt is an effective option for preventing and removing ice from sidewalks, driveways and stairs, but it isn’t suitable for every surface.
  • Ice melt salt chemically reacts with certain materials, accelerates freeze-thaw cycles and alters surface moisture levels to cause damage.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Family Handyman's Editorial Process.

Avoid damaging salt-sensitive outdoor surfaces with these expert-backed suggestions.

Recent findings suggest that ice melt salt is an effective option for preventing and removing ice from sidewalks, driveways and stairs, but it isn’t suitable for every surface. Applying ice melt to certain materials can cause significant damage and should be avoided. Ahead, learn which surfaces are most vulnerable to damage from ice melt, why it happens and what safer alternatives you can use to keep outdoor areas free from ice.

Ice melt salt chemically reacts with certain materials, accelerates freeze-thaw cycles and alters surface moisture levels to cause damage. The type of damage will depend on the surface and how it interacts with ice melt.

Ice melt contains rock salt, calcium chloride and/or magnesium chloride to melt ice faster and at lower temperatures. While all melting salt is corrosive and can damage outdoor surfaces, ice melt products can react differently than rock salt alone.

Ice melt seeps deeply into porous cement-based materials. The calcium chloride in ice melt can react with elements of concrete or brick to form calcium oxychloride crystals. As the crystals grow, they generate extreme pressure that can cause cracks, surface spalling and crumbling.

In a recent development, de-icing products accelerate freeze-thaw cycles in porous cement-based surfaces, causing them to break down. “It makes the freezing and thawing cycle more aggressive, which is what causes the surface to break up,” Murphy says.

According to recent reports, though less damaging than rock salt, ice melt can still contribute to deterioration. Calcium chloride and magnesium chloride attract and retain moisture, increasing the potential for freeze-thaw damage.

Conversely, ice melt draws moisture out of organic materials, causing them to dry out. Over time, this moisture loss can lead to warping, cracking, splitting and other forms of deterioration.

Ice melt accelerates metal oxidation to create rust. It can corrode rebar embedded in concrete, potentially causing cracks and structural damage, as well as rusting exposed metal stairs and railings.

It’s best to avoid applying salt to these salt-sensitive surfaces.

“Fresh concrete is the most vulnerable because it takes weeks to fully cure, so salt on the surface will cause the top few millimeters to flake off,” Murphy indicates. To be safe, avoid salting new concrete for the first season.

“Cracked concrete opens up for water to get inside, and salt in the water will only make that worse because it will freeze and thaw more aggressively,” Murphy says.

All ice melt products will damage hard-scape surfaces due to chemical reactions and freeze-thaw cycles. “If you are using them, use them sparingly and remove them as soon as possible to decrease continuous exposure for your hardscape areas,” Zurcher states.

Natural stone like limestone and flagstone can react to ice melt compounds. The porous surface is vulnerable to damaging freeze-thaw cycles as well.

Harsh de-icers can damage dyed, painted or stamped concrete surfaces by breaking down color pigments.

Metal stairs and railings will rapidly rust when salt is applied to them, so it’s best to avoid it.

Industry observers note that ice melt draws moisture from wood, causing cracking, warping and raised fibers. It also degrades paint and stain and leaves behind chalky white salt stains.

Sand: Sand doesn’t melt ice, but does provide traction to prevent slips.

Wood ash: Instead of throwing away wood ash, use it as a salt alternative to melt ice and also provide improved traction.

It has been revealed that electric mats: Installed before cold weather sets in, electric melting mats warm up and prevent ice from ever forming. These can be very effective on stairs and sidewalks.

According to recent reports, weed torch: Weed torches are handy when you need to melt a lot of ice swiftly. Do not use one to melt ice on wood and avoid painted or stained concrete as well.

“The best way to reduce damage from these chemicals is to shovel snow as soon as possible,” Zurcher says, so you can use less of them. Use ice melt sparingly, and only as directed. A handful is enough to treat three square yards. Instead of using ice melt alone, mix a small amount with sand to treat surfaces.

It has been revealed that regular sealing protects cement-based products. “Reseal every three to five years to make sure no water can get in, salty or not,” Murphy says. Additionally, use chloride-free de-icing products, or those labelled as “concrete-safe”.

Newly poured concrete is the most vulnerable to salt damage, but all concrete surfaces will experience damage with enough prolonged exposure to salt.

Industry observers note that it depends on the extent of the damage. Major cracks and breakage mean concrete needs to be removed and repoured, Zurcher says, while surface damage could be skim-coated, with potentially limited results.

Pet-safe products will have similar effects on hardscape areas, Zurcher says, as they still contain salt.

I’ve tested a lot of air purifiers, and most look like appliances I’d rather tuck out of sight in a corner. The Dupray Bloom Air Purifier is different. But I also wanted to know whether the Bloom’s unusual design would interfere with its primary job of filtering the air.

Recent findings suggest that absolutely, and that’s what makes the Bloom so appealing. The top features a removable planting pot with a root tray that helps keep roots above excess water. I chose a small fiddle-leaf fig, and once it was planted, the Bloom looked more like a decorative planter than an air-cleaning appliance.

There is one thing I’d caution buyers about: The planter doesn’t have drainage holes. The root tray provides some separation from standing water, but it isn’t a substitute for proper watering. I’d recommend using an olla, a small porous automatic watering vessel that slowly releases moisture into the soil. It’s a good option for keeping the plant watered without repeatedly pouring water into a pot that can’t drain.

I also appreciated that the planter lifts completely out. That means I can move the plant for maintenance or repotting without having to move the entire purifier. And when it’s time to replace the round HEPA filter, I can remove the planter, turn the unit over, and access the filter from the bottom.

Industry observers note that behind its decorative design, the Bloom is a serious air purifier. It uses an H13 HEPA filter with activated carbon to capture airborne particles, including dust, pollen, and pet dander, while helping reduce odors. Dupray rates it as capable of capturing 99.97 percent of particles as small as 0.1 micron.

Recent findings suggest that one feature I particularly liked was the stretchy fabric prefilter. It slips snugly over the purifier’s base, creating a smooth, modern appearance while catching larger airborne particles before they reach the HEPA filter. It’s washable, too, and Dupray offers replacement prefilters in different colors.

The Bloom also has an AutoDetect mode that monitors air quality and adjusts the fan speed. There are three manual fan settings, along with a sleep mode for quieter operation. Dupray rates its lowest noise level at just 24 decibels, making it suitable for bedrooms and other living spaces where a loud fan would be distracting.

According to recent reports, it’s remarkably simple. The removable planter makes the HEPA filter accessible, and the fabric prefilter stretches on and off without clips or complicated fasteners.

Another smart touch is the universal power adapter. It comes with interchangeable plug configurations for the U.S., U.K., and Europe. That’s not something I typically see included with an air purifier.

According to recent reports, my only complaint—and it’s minor—is the digital control display. The symbols for Auto, Sleep, and the fan-speed bars looked slightly blurry to me. I could still identify them and operate the purifier, but a sharper display would have been easier to read. Or I might need a new prescription for glasses.

At $249.99, the Bloom isn’t the cheapest way to get HEPA filtration, but its design sets it apart from the usual boxy models. It’s particularly appealing for living rooms, bedrooms, and home offices where an ordinary air purifier might detract from the decor.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Avoid injury with these expert-backed snow shoveling safety tips.
  • With autumn in full swing, it’s time to start thinking about preparing for the looming winter months.
  • Shoveling may seem simple, but can lead to strains, pulls and cardiac events if not done properly.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Family Handyman's Editorial Process.

Avoid injury with these expert-backed snow shoveling safety tips.

With autumn in full swing, it’s time to start thinking about preparing for the looming winter months. If you live in a snow-prone climate, this means getting out the shovels, salt and snowblower before the first flakes fly. Even if you’re not new to shoveling, it’s worth learning how to do it safely, as injuries can occur at any time.

Shoveling may seem simple, but can lead to strains, pulls and cardiac events if not done properly. Ahead, learn expert-backed tips to shovel snow the right (and safe) way with insights from cardiologist Dr. Bradley Serwer.

The safest way to shovel snow is to push it as much as possible and avoid lifting. If you must lift snow to remove it, bend at the knees and lift with your legs instead of your back.

“The most crucial tool when preparing to shovel snow is good common sense,” Serwer says. “Dress appropriately and consider the risks of the job at hand.”.

Dress in layers that allow you to remove or open up a layer of clothing as you warm up to avoid getting overheated. Opt for a moisture wicking base layer, a mid-weight layer and a jacket that is wind-resistant and waterproof. Wear warm, waterproof gloves, a hat, warm socks and thick-soled winter boots. For particularly cold temperatures and high winds, add ski goggles and a balaclava to protect sensitive facial skin.

According to recent reports, consider a quick warm up and stretch session for a safer shoveling session. Get your blood pumping with some light activity like jumping jacks, walking in place or climbing up and down the stairs in your home. Gently stretch major muscle groups before heading outside.

Sources indicate that snow shovels are not all created equal. For safer shoveling, choose one that is less demanding on your back, joints and heart. Ergonomic shovels feature a curved handle that reduces back strain when lifting. Snow plow shovels are meant to push snow only, not lift it. And battery-powered shovels act like mini-snowblowers to quickly remove snow without any manual input.

In a recent development, keep your back straight, bend at the knees and use your legs to lift snow for safer shoveling. Keep the loaded shovel close to your body, then, without twisting, turn your body toward the direction you place the snow. If snow is wet or deeper than six inches, remove it in smaller layers, rather than one heavy shovelful.

“It is often underestimated what kind of physical workload is required to shovel a substantial amount of snow,” Serwer notes. That’s why it’s important to pace yourself, stop regularly and initiative ahead to avoid overexertion. Opt for a slow and steady pace, especially if you’re typically sedentary. Rigorous snow shoveling will swiftly lead to overexertion and cardiac strain. Going slow allows you to focus on safe shoveling technique, preventing possible muscle strains and pulls. Stay well-hydrated when shoveling and take regular breaks to allow your heart rate to return to normal and your muscles to recover.

Stop shoveling if you’re experiencing cardiac distress, cold-related conditions, dehydration or back strain.

Recent findings suggest that “Shoveling snow can be a very strenuous activity, placing notable strain on the cardiovascular system,” Serwer notes. Know the signs of a heart attack before picking up a shovel, like chest pressure, shortness of breath, nausea and radiating arm pain. Stop immediately if you experience these symptoms and seek medical help. “Hire someone else to shovel, especially if you are at a high cardiac risk,” Serwer says.

Industry observers note that dress in layers and cover exposed skin in freezing temperatures and wind. Even with these efforts, frostbite and hypothermia are real risks. Frostbite begins in extremities like fingers and toes, and exposed facial skin. Early signs include pale, cold skin and prickling or numb sensations. Hypothermia happens when core body temperatures drop too low and begins with clumsiness, foggy thinking, fatigue and intense shivering. Stop immediately and go inside to warm up if you experience these symptoms.

“It is very easy to become dehydrated while working in cold climates,” Serwer says, as the human body suppresses the thirst response and dry winter air pulls additional moisture from our bodies. Notice signs of dehydration like fatigue, dry throat, cracked lips or a headache. “Dehydration is often overlooked, and people don’t replace the fluids as needed,” Serwer adds. Stop and take regular water breaks and continue drinking fluids for the remainder of the day if you notice these signs.

According to recent reports, shoveling puts strain on your spine and back, and can lead to serious, long term injuries like herniated disks, sciatica and lower back strains if you’re not careful. Beyond always lifting with your legs, stop shoveling if you feel the early signs of spine and back strain. These include a dull, aching in your lower back, sharp pain when bending or twisting, muscle cramping or shooting pains.

It is safer to push snow rather than lift it.

Individuals with heart disease, obesity, diabetes and high blood pressure should not shovel snow. Those over 45 years old should also exercise caution.

You must be fast, Kagan said. I was then, I joked. I was 79 now and slow.

Justice Kagan clerked for Justice Marshall, who apparently never discussed the sourcing for The Brethren.

Is all of this known about The Brethren? Kagan asked. I didn't have an answer so instead I dived into Blackmun's role in Roe v. Wade and how he had drafted the opinion at the Mayo Clinic library. "I thought the leak of the Dobbs decision was a public service," I told her, referencing the decision that had overturned Roe the previous year. I can't say I agree with that, Kagan said. Why do you think it's a public service? Well, the court took away a right that had been there for 50 years. The public needed to know so there could be a debate. Kagan didn't say anything.

I find it odd that Kagan stated nothing in response. This is not the sort of statement that could trigger a recusal. She might have said "that debate nearly got my colleague assassinated." But she stayed silent.

Industry observers note that I said from reporting more than 50 years on 10 presidents, I thought there was such a concentration of power in the presidency. Too much power.

She nodded. It's why Trump was able to get away with so much, I said. Kagan did not respond. Then I said, there's too much power in the Supreme Court maybe. She noticeably reacted to that, her head held a little higher, her posture stiffening. Her only reply was, "That's interesting.".

Sources indicate that she mustered a response here, but not to the leak question. Interesting?

"Are you happy on the court?" I asked her. No, I'm not, given the situation, Kagan replied. I was surprised at her candor.

Kagan likely didn't think she would be quoted.

As we parted ways, she smiled warmly and said she respected my work and I said I respected hers. Late that night I recorded a detailed voice memo of my conversation with Kagan for my assistant to transcribe. It is hard to tell who was interviewing who.

The Breyer anecdote is far shorter.

On Saturday, October 21, 2023, Elsa and I attended a dinner for the 50th anniversary of the Saturday Night Massacre hosted by the former Watergate special prosecutors at the WilmerHale law firm in downtown Washington. The main speaker was retired Supreme Court justice Stephen Breyer, who had been a junior Watergate prosecutor. Elsa sat next to Breyer at the dinner before switching seats with me. He had served 28 years on the Supreme Court and told her he was "forced out" so someone younger could take his place.

According to recent reports, no one forced him out. He has life tenure. Instead, Breyer surrendered to the pressure. So much for judicial independence. Justices Alito and Thomas are often charged with being MAGA partisans, but they exhibited robust independence from political forces.

Woodward offers this anecdote about the Thomas confirmation hearing:.

Later Gray told me it took five years for Clarence Thomas to recover. Justice Thomas's wife, Ginni Thomas, a conservative activist, approached me at a conference in Washington one day. She said after the hearings her husband was never really a whole person again. He hardened. Many conservatives, including attorney general for George H. W. Bush and for Donald Trump, Bill Barr, have said the hearings pushed Thomas to the hard right.

I couldn't find any references to other current justices.

I will read the chapters on The Brethren with interest.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Family Handyman's Editorial Process.

Those roadside scales do more than weigh semitrucks. Here’s what inspectors check and what happens when a truck pulls into a weigh station.

In a recent development, drivers pass truck weigh stations all the time, but few know everything these stations do or what happens when a truck pulls in. Once a semitruck exits and rejoins the highway, it’s hard to tell what goes on in between.

Learn what happens when a truck pulls in, what inspectors look for, and why some drivers can keep going.

Industry observers note that truck weigh stations help states enforce weight limits and spot safety problems. Trucks can weigh too much overall or carry too much weight on certain axles, putting extra strain on roads and bridges. On the Interstate System, the standard federal limits are 80,000 pounds gross vehicle weight, 20,000 pounds on a single axle, and 34,000 pounds on a tandem axle. Federal bridge weight rules and certain exceptions can also affect how much a truck may legally carry. Limits on other roads can vary.

According to recent reports, rules vary by state. “Some require all commercial motor vehicles to stop, while others require only those above a certain weight to stop,” according to the Federal Highway Administration. “Ultimately, States must certify that they are enforcing their weight limits on certain highways in order not to jeopardize their receipt of Federal highway funds.”.

Industry observers note that drivers who pull in follow signs directing them to a scale, where their trucks are weighed either while moving slowly or at a complete stop. If the weight is within the limits, they may be cleared to leave. Inspectors may still pull a truck aside for a closer look even when its weight is fine, based on screening results, visible defects, or random selection. An overweight truck may also be inspected further.

Inspectors may check a truck’s tires, brakes, lights, and cargo, along with the driver’s records. They may also review credentials and permits, such as registration and fuel-tax paperwork, along with the driver’s hours-of-service logs. “There are eight levels of inspections ranging from the Level I Inspection, which evaluates both the driver and vehicle, to inspection levels with a more specific area of focus, such as Level VI for radioactive materials and Level VIII for electronic inspections,” according to the Commercial Vehicle Safety Alliance.

In a recent development, drivers of overweight trucks may receive a citation or have to move or remove some cargo before leaving. The exact consequences vary by state and violation.

According to recent reports, more serious safety problems, like faulty brakes, can put a truck or driver out of service. A truck placed out of service can’t return to the road until the problem is fixed. Drivers placed out of service must wait until their restrictions end.

Some trucks can skip the stop altogether through electronic bypass programs. These programs use safety records and other information to determine whether a driver can continue without entering the station. Drivers still have to follow any signs or signals telling them to stop.

Recent findings suggest that at $2,395 for the king size I tested, the Perfectly Snug Smart Topper is absolutely a luxury purchase. After sleeping on it for 2 months during a Florida summer, however, I can say that its temperature-control technology delivers. This 2-inch topper uses fans, airflow, heating elements, and temperature sensors to regulate each side of the bed independently, creating a surprisingly effective way to stay comfortable throughout the night. While some aspects of the design could use a little more refinement, the actual cooling performance left me impressed.

Industry observers note that installation was straightforward. I unpacked the vacuum-sealed topper, laid it over my king mattress, added my usual fitted sheet, and plugged it in. The power supply is fairly big, but I had no trouble tucking it down behind my headboard. The cables emerge from the head of the topper, which is worth keeping in mind if you tend to stretch your arms overhead while sleeping. As for comfort, the topper has an unusual feel at first—slightly firm but with enough give to stay comfortable. Its internal mesh structure allows air to circulate beneath you, and the effect is immediately noticeable, even on lower settings.

The cooling performance is easily my favorite feature. Even at level 3, I could feel a gentle, pleasant stream of cool air underneath me, which was especially welcome during warm Florida nights. The one trade-off is fan noise, which becomes quite noticeable at higher settings. Anything above level 5 was too loud for my sleeping preferences, but I found an easy workaround using the app’s scheduling feature. I’d run the cooling at a higher setting for about an hour before bedtime, then lower it to level 3 when I climbed into bed. This gave me the best of both worlds: a wonderfully cool mattress at bedtime and gentle, nearly silent cooling throughout the night.

It has been revealed that there are a few areas where I’d love to see Perfectly Snug make improvements, especially considering the premium price. The power supply and small side-mounted control panel are functional but have a fairly basic appearance. I also occasionally brushed against the fans positioned at the foot of the topper, which could briefly interrupt their operation (making a noticeable “you’ve just stopped a fan from moving” type of buzzing sound). The companion app was another underwhelming aspect of the experience. While it offers useful features like scheduling and temperature adjustments, its interface feels super dated and could benefit from a much more polished, intuitive design. None of these complications prevented me from enjoying the topper, but they’re details I’d expect to see addressed at this price point.

Ultimately, the Perfectly Snug Smart Topper gets the most crucial thing right: keeping your bed at a comfortable temperature. I enjoyed slipping into a perfectly cooled bed each night, and the subtle airflow on lower settings noticeably improved my sleep comfort. It’s an innovative product with plenty to offer, particularly for hot sleepers or couples with different temperature preferences. Although the fan noise and a few less-refined design elements keep it from feeling like a truly premium experience, the core technology is admirable. With some thoughtful improvements, this could be an outstanding luxury sleep upgrade.

#136060. Setting the Record Straight On Senator Cornyn And The N.D. Tex. Seat (Updated)

Setting the Record Straight On Senator Cornyn And The N.D. Tex. Seat (Updated)

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1811 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Reason

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • At the outset of President Trump's second term, there were a number of vacant district court seats throughout Texas.
  • Sources indicate that up to this point, none of the vacancies in the Northern District of Texas were tapped.
  • But there were still two open seats.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

At the outset of President Trump's second term, there were a number of vacant district court seats throughout Texas. A reasonable person might have predicted that given two Republican senators, those seats would be filled quickly, but no such luck. The first nomination--Nicholas Ganjei for S.D.Tex--was not made until November 2025. Yes, while Missouri quickly filled all the seats, Texas lagged behind. Two more nominations in the Western District were made in January 2026--Andrew Davis for the Austin seat and Chis Wolfe for the Waco seat. It's worth noting that both Ganjei and Davis served as Chief Counsel for Senator Cruz. And the story of the Waco seat is enough for another post. In April 2026, two more nominations were made for S.D. Tex. seats in the Valley: John Marck and Arthur Jones.

Sources indicate that up to this point, none of the vacancies in the Northern District of Texas were tapped. Finally, in May 2026, Kasdin Mitchell was nominated to one of the seats in N.D. Tex. At that time, Angela Colmenero was tapped for another seat in Houston. Four more months would lapse. In September, Richard Bennett was nominated for a seat in Houston and Courtney Coker was nominated for a seat in Dallas.

But there were still two open seats. The critical vacancy was the Western District of Texas seat in Austin, which had remained open for some time. Virtually all of the litigation against the state government is filed in Austin. And, for reasons that continue to elude me, David Ezra, a senior judge from Hawaii, brings the Aloha Spirit to muck up Texas jurisprudence.

Shortly after the midterm election, President Trump nominated Justice James Sullivan of the Texas Supreme Court for the Austin seat. Around the same time, Trump nominated Elliot Gaiser for the remaining N.D. Tex. in Dallas. Ultimately, Senator Cornyn would block Gaiser's nomination, and urged the White House to nominate Steve Fahey. That's where thing stand now.

In a recent development, many people, even those in Texas, cannot make sense of this situation. Why on earth did it take so long to fill all of these seats? Why did nominations for the final two seats only come after the election? Why did Trump pick Gaiser if Cornyn had objections?

Let me try to set the record straight on a few matters here.

Recent findings suggest that traditionally, Texas District court nominees have gone through something called the Federal Judicial Evaluation Committee (FJEC). Senators Cornyn and Cruz have used this structure to allow local attorneys (now about 30) to make recommendations on potential judicial candidates. The committee will screen applications, conduct interview, and recommend finalists to the Senators. Generally, if both senators sign off on a finalist, they recommend the name to the White House. At that point, the White House will conduct an interview, and if things work out, a nomination is made. I hedge slightly, because sometimes the process goes in a different order. It can happen that the White House really likes a particular candidate, and speaks to them in parallel, or even before the FJEC process goes through. But FJEC remains a central cog in any district court nomination.

For more than a year, there has been something of a standoff concerning the N.D. Tex. seat. There were two relevant finalists from FJEC. The first was Michael Berry, a Marine Veteran, longtime attorney with the First Liberty Institute, and--perhaps most importantly--former Chief Counsel to Senator Cruz. The second was Steve Fahey, a lawyer I did not know. He was an assistant United States Attorney until 2021, and now has a solo private practice. I'm told one of his most significant case was seeking a writ of coram nobis to protect an illegal alien from deportation. (The petition was denied.).

According to recent reports, senator Cornyn blocked Berry. Or to be more precise, Cornyn's Chief Counsel, Franci Becker, blocked Berry. The exact reason is not entirely clear. I've heard some rumors that Becker blames Berry for blocking another district court nominee, but that never happened. Senator Cruz supported that nominee. The White House found problems in that nom's record that would have made confirmation impossible. Ultimately, she withdrew from the search, and took a lucrative in-house position. Another explanation is that Becker, and Cornyn, opposed Berry because he was too conservative. Whatever the reasons, Berry had deep ties to Texas. The White House had interviewed Berry, and was prepared to make the nomination, but Cornyn kept saying no. The Washington Examiner reports on this story.

What about Fahey? I'm told that Cruz never actually blocked Fahey, but the White House had reservations about the nominee--especially his work defending illegal aliens. Ultimately, the decision was made to just let the seat stay open and it would be filled once Cornyn is out of office. The Austin seat was vital, as it involves so much state-wide litigation, but the Dallas division seats are interchangeable. This is not Amarillo or Wichita Falls. Indeed, even if Paxton were to lose the election, the Senate was likely to stay in Republican control, and a deal could be made with Senator Talarico for the Dallas seat. Alas, the election day bloodbath changed things.

Sources indicate that the Sullivan nomination for the Austin seat was made quite quickly, even though it had been in the works for a while. Sullivan had already gone through the background check, as well as the FJEC approval. But what about Elliot Gaiser? It is true that Gaiser did not go through FJEC, but he had something very notable: a recent FBI background check and Senate confirmation. He could (in theory) be slotted into the final confirmation hearing planned for November 18.

Sources indicate that despite my best efforts, Senator Cornyn blocked Gaiser's nomination. Cornyn (or at least someone on his staff) put out this social media post to explain his actions:.

Recent findings suggest that if President Trump wanted to fill a judicial vacancy in Dallas, why did he wait until after the midterms to nominate someone? The seat has been vacant since 2025. Then, without any consultation, he nominates a non-Texan with little connection to the Lone Star State, with no trial court experience, and who has not been appropriately vetted for a lifetime job. The Senate has a constitutional responsibility to provide "advise and consent," which is impossible without consultation.

Sources indicate that still, I would like to work with the President to fill the seat while we still have a Senate majority. I have forwarded an outstanding candidate who was highly rated by Senator Cruz's and my bipartisan Federal Judicial Evaluation Committee, and who has now been interviewed by White House Counsel. All that is needed is an FBI background check with they stand ready to do on a timely basis.

Back to you, Mr. President. Time is of the essence.

This post is misleading. Why did Trump wait until after the midterms to nominate someone? The short answer is that Cornyn blocked the White House's and Cruz's preferred candidate, and the White House did not want to pick Cornyn's candidate. That's how things work. Senators can withhold consent by not returning a blue slip. But they can't force the White House to make a nomination they don't wish to make. The White House then tried a list-ditch effort to get someone into the seat before the upcoming Congress concluded. I'm sure the administration was hoping that Senator Cornyn would realize that a filled seat is better than an empty seat, but he refused, and blocked Gaiser. Moreover, Cornyn refused to even meet with Gaiser, so he is no position to complain about a "lack of consultation." FJEC could have performed a review of Gaiser on short notice, but it was never convened.

Cornyn notes Fahey was "was highly rated by Senator Cruz's and my bipartisan Federal Judicial Evaluation Committee." But that does not mean Senator Cruz himself approved of Fahey. Indeed, Senator Cruz can still withhold a blue slip of Fahey. That comeuppance would be just, after Cornyn blocked both Berry and Gaiser unreasonably. Cornyn has earned no favors at this point--especially after cursing at Cruz on the Senate floor and calling him a "fragile thing" on social media. After the events of the past few weeks, I think James Talarico would be a more trustworthy partner on nominees than Cornyn. Remember, Cornyn aided and abetted the spiking of Lee Rudofsky's nomination to the Eighth Circuit. Soon enough, Judge Ada Brown's NDTX seat will become open--either through resignation or impeachment. I can see a deal being made with Cruz gets one of the Dallas seats and Talarico gets the other. All Cornyn could do that point is grouse.

The bigger problem is that there is no time left for a hearing. The November 18 hearing was the end of the show. Cornyn's stunt is now putting pressure on Senator Grassley to break even more China by holding a December nomination hearing. There is no reason that Grassley should give Cornyn this courtesy--especially after the recent stunts Cornyn has pulled.

According to recent reports, this post is based on my best understanding of some complex deliberations over the course of nearly two years. If you spot any errors, please send me an email.

Upgrade: Tuesday evening, the press secretary from Senator Cornyn's post reached out and said "It's inaccurate to say that Franci Becker is responsible for blocking Mike Berry's nomination." She asked me to post a statement, which I will do:.

It has been revealed that attributable to a Cornyn spokesperson, Franci Becker did not block Mike Berry's nomination, as staff in Senate offices do not have the authority to make decisions about a nominee, and the claims in this story were not corroborated by Sen. Cornyn's office.

Of course, the ultimate decision to sign a blue slip belongs to the Senator. In any office, a staffer cannot take a final action. So in a hyper-technical sense, no staffer is capable of blocking any nominee. But Chief Counsels routinely make decisions about candidates that their senators defer to.

What the statement does not say is far more key than what it actually says. There is no denial along the lines of, "Franci Becker played no role in Mike Berry not receiving a blue slip." We set up a leafy obstacle course and tested each of these tools for at least an hour. We wanted to see how well they piled leaves (if applicable), and how they reduced leaf piles for disposal or reuse in the yard. Throughout the process, we recorded our observations on a scoring rubric. We tracked measurables such as tool weight, charge time, run time, and how rapidly a vacuum loaded its collection bag without clogging. We also noted subjective observations regarding operating comfort, ease of use, and perceived value. Finally, we used the scoring rubric to assign award titles.

According to recent reports, leaf vacuums come in various types and with different-size collection bags. There are also three power source types—gas, electric, and cordless/battery—with each option affecting runtime and suction. Take a look below at some important factors to help determine the motor type, power, and design that will work best for you.

Leaf vacuums are made in a few types, and some kinds work better in certain situations and setups than others.

Like lawn mowers, leaf vacuums are available in electric- and gas-powered versions.

To figure out the power of a leaf vacuum, check the product description for two numbers: mph and CFM. The mph stands for miles per hour—in this case, referring to how quickly air is suctioned into the unit and through the tube. Most units run between 110 and 180 mph, although some may reach extremes of 250 mph or so.

According to recent reports, somewhat more crucial than airspeed, however, is CFM. This describes how much air moves through the vacuum in the span of 60 seconds, indicating how powerful the unit is. While mph provides an idea of how quickly leaves can go through the tube, CFM indicates how much can go through all at once.

Industry observers note that the CFM rankings for leaf vacuums range between 150 to 600. A unit with a CFM under 200 may be all that’s needed to clean up an apartment balcony or a small yard, but for larger areas, it may be desirable to invest in a unit with higher CFM.

Saunders recommends a leaf vacuum with a strong motor “that can really get the job done.” He adds, “Something like a 12-amp electric motor, which you’ll find in some top models, will give you the suction power you need to handle a good amount of leaves without getting bogged down.”.

Industry observers note that the runtime of a battery-powered leaf vacuum can limit the amount of work that can be done. Most models offer at least 20 to 30 minutes of runtime on the highest power levels. At lower levels, the battery may run for 45 minutes or more.

Industry observers note that battery-powered models that include two or more interchangeable batteries can increase the available work time. While one battery is in use, the other battery charges. Charge times vary from 1.5 to 3 hours and sometimes longer depending on the battery size. The amount of work may still be limited with interchangeable batteries, but it will provide more work time than a single battery.

Industry observers note that some manufacturers provide batteries that are interchangeable with the brand’s other power tools. In these cases, buying power tools of the same brand can add to the number of batteries available. Ultimately, that can extend possible work time even more.

It has been revealed that some leaf vacuums offer bells and whistles beyond simple suction. In fact, most vacuums these days are actually leaf blowers with a vacuum function. That provides extra use options with a single tool.

Recent findings suggest that leaf vacuums are best suited for smaller outdoor spaces, like those surrounding garden apartments and duplexes. Some models also offer a mulching option, which is great for repurposing leaves into healthy plant beds.

A leaf vacuum’s mix of features and design can make it easier or harder to use. Bag size, for example, determines how often it will need to be emptied. Larger bags mean less frequent emptying, but they can be awkward and heavy to carry.

Weight also affects ease of use. Gas-powered leaf vacuums weigh the most, though some battery-powered models are almost as heavy. For those with a large yard, gas power makes sense because it can keep a consistent high power throughout the whole yard.

In a recent development, however, for those with smaller yards, the lightweight nature of a handheld or a battery-powered model can be more comfortable. Models with a backpack bag combine the lighter weight of a handheld leaf vacuum with the convenience of a backpack.

According to recent reports, ergonomics is also something to take into consideration. “You’re going to be using this tool for a while, so it needs to be comfortable,” Saunders claims. “Lightweight models are easier on the arms and back, especially if you’re working in a large yard. Features like an ergonomically designed tube can also make a big difference by reducing strain.”.

Recent findings suggest that finally, there are controls to consider. Trigger switches and on/off buttons directly on the handle are easier to use. This allows you to turn the machine on or off with one hand. Toolless conversion for hybrid models can also add to ease of use.

Leaf vacuums aren’t complicated once you understand how they work and what features are needed for specific jobs. However, since they aren’t as common as leaf blowers, you might still find yourself scratching your head as you look at the specs. Here, we answer some of the most common questions about leaf vacuums to help you make the right choice.

According to recent reports, A leaf vacuum is the best machine for picking up leaves. Choose one that matches your yard size and typical leaf volume. Battery-powered handheld models work best for small yards with a moderate amount of leaves. Electric and gas models offer longer running times and a larger collection bag capacity for larger areas and heavier leaf cover.

In a recent development, A leaf vacuum needs a minimum rating of 340 CFM and 150 mph to pick up dry material effectively. Leaf removal equipment rated above 500 CFM and 180 mph is best for large areas and wet leaves and debris.

Yes, a lawn vacuum will effectively pick up dry and clumped grass clippings.

Sources indicate that no, leaf vacuums are not designed to clean gutters. They don’t offer the required suction or reach to do the job.

To switch a dual-purpose leaf blower/vac from blower to vacuum mode, remove the blower tube and intake guard; then attach the vacuum tube (to the air intake) and the collection bag (where the blower tube came off). Check the owner’s manual for specific instructions.

Yes, leaf vacuums can be noisy, especially those with gas engines. Some models can reach 90 decibels. However, those powered by rechargeable batteries are much quieter, in the 60 to 80 decibel range.

In a recent development, to clean an outdoor vacuum for leaves, first turn it off and disconnect the power cord or battery. Empty the collection bag, including anything that may not easily dump out. Remove and unclog the suction nozzle, and clear any debris from the impeller.

Leaf vacuums will last 8 to 10 years or longer with routine maintenance.

Leaf vacuum prices range from about $100 to more than $1000, depending on the design and size.

Family Handyman's Editorial Process.

GTA6 let's you take a break from a life of crime to make some much-needed home repairs on Jason and Lucia's house.

Sources indicate that just in case your algorithm is different from mine, here’s some news: Grand Theft Auto 6 officially released today. After 13 years of waiting, fans of the open-world action-adventure video game series can finally dive into a new, richly detailed and fully realized virtual world. Boot up the game, and you’ll find yourself faced with surprising realism, a world of crime, and the ability to do just about whatever you want. That’s right, even… DIY home improvement jobs?

It has been revealed that yep, you’re reading that right. As part of its commitment to realism, GTA developer Rockstar Games has given players the ability to do some honest-to-goodness, roll-up-your-sleeves-and-get-to-work home improvement virtually.

And it’s not just a short cutscene where you see the house magically go from disrepair to fully fixed up. You, as the player, have to actually do the work, whether you’re drywalling, painting, or roofing. Luckily, it’s just a video game because the game is also set in a fictional version of Florida in the summer, which is probably one of the last places on earth you’d want to be stuck doing any sort of construction work.

Let’s take a look at a few of the home improvement jobs done by GTA6‘s Jason Duval and see if his work meets Family Handyman’s standards.

With his lady friend Lucia on the way back from prison, Jason decides to fix up the place… including the unfinished framing in the center of his living room. Luckily, Jason knows how to hang drywall. The gameplay represents the job pretty accurately— Jason holds the drywall in place and screws it into the studs with an impact driver. We don’t get to see any taping or mudding, though. 7/10.

Industry observers note that next, we’ll inspect whether Jason should perhaps prioritize a career as a painter over his life of crime. The painting section is also pretty accurate to the average DIY painting experience. Jason has to choose between three different color options before pouring the paint into a tray and using a roller to paint the wall. It’s pretty boring, which is honestly just like painting in real life — so bonus points for immersive realism. 8/10.

One of the first things Jason knows he has to fix before Lucia arrives is the massive hole in his roof that’s letting in a near-constant drip of rain. Luckily, like a lot of DIYers, he has some roofing experience, a cordless nail gun and a stack of shingles just lying around for some reason. Again, this section is pretty realistic. If gamers want the full Florida roofing experience, though, they’ll have to crank their heaters to maximum or perhaps play the game in a sauna. 6/10.

Sources indicate that look, I get it. The Grand Theft Auto series is about living out fantasies, providing gamers a sandbox where they can virtually experience the impossible.

According to recent reports, but still… “House repairs complete” is a bridge too far. Ask any DIYer, and they will tell you no house is ever fully repaired. Pretending home improvement work could ever be finished is just not realistic and really took me out of the experience. 3/10.

Overall, the game is cool. But to be honest, I’m not sure what the point is now that the house repairs are complete.

I’ve tested several Aiper cleaners over the years, and the Aiper Scuba V3 Ultra feels like a natural evolution of the brand’s previous models. I ran it through repeated cleaning cycles in my 8,500-gallon saltwater pool in Florida, where leaves, bugs, fine debris, and the occasional patch of algae give pool robots plenty to deal with. Setup was super simple: The Aiper app connected quickly, the robot updated without any fuss, and I had it in the water about 15 minutes after opening the box.

What impressed me right away was just how much the Scuba V3 Ultra can do in one cleaning cycle. Plenty of the robotic pool cleaners we’ve tested at Bob Vila handle floors, walls, and the waterline, but only a select few can also skim floating debris from the surface. That matters in my open-air pool, which regularly collects bugs and leaves. Anything the Aiper actually reaches gets cleaned extremely well.

According to recent reports, the MicroMesh filter is another highlight. It traps extremely fine material, including algae and sediment that can slip through coarser filter baskets. Cleaning that ultra-fine layer takes a little more effort—I usually spend a few minutes thoroughly rinsing it with a hose and then leave it out to dry—but that’s a fair trade-off for how much fine material it captures. The app is also among the better pool-cleaner apps I’ve used, and I like getting a notification when the cleaning cycle is finished. The robot then floats neatly near the pool edge for retrieval.

Recent findings suggest that where the V3 Ultra disappointed me was its claim of shallow-area cleaning. Aiper notes it can work in water down to about 7.9 inches deep, but my sun shelf is apparently too shallow for it to clean reliably. I still have to brush debris from the shelf into the main pool and let the robot collect it there. It also won’t clean my pool steps. For a $2,300 machine marketed around near-total pool coverage, those are significant omissions—especially since sun shelves have become so common in newer pools.

Still, I’m a fan of the Scuba V3 Ultra overall. My older Aiper cleaner has been running reliably for close to two years, which gives me more confidence in the brand than I’d have from a short-term test alone. The voice assistant is useful without being obnoxious, retrieval is simple, filtration is excellent, and cleaning performance everywhere the robot can reach is phenomenal. I’m still waiting for the robot that will truly clean every inch of my pool, but the Scuba V3 Ultra gets closer than most.

There’s no place like home for the holidays. As it gets closer to the most magical time of the year, stores are stocked with decorations significant and small, and figuring out how you want your home to look can be a little overwhelming. Thankfully, experts in the home decor space are sharing their seasonal tips to help you get ready.

HGTV’s Jonathan Scott shared a video with a few Christmas decorating hacks he and his partner, Zooey Deschanel, use in their home.

“I like it to be a little bit nostalgic, a little bit fun, and a whole lot of holiday spirit,” Scott says.

In a recent development, there’s no one right way to decorate for Christmas, and even if so that doesn’t mean you should stick to the conventional script, according to Scott. “There are lots of different rules when decorating for the holidays, but of course, as we know, rules are meant to be broken,” Scott says. “So it really depends on your comfort level.”.

Here are some of Scott’s hacks:.

It has been revealed that even the nicest artificial trees can look a little too perfect. Scott’s trick is to stuff a few extra branches into the tree, leaving some sticking out at random. He also adds more lights, including larger bulbs, even though his tree is already pre-lit.

According to recent reports, scott has been collecting nutcrackers for years, and yes, he even names them. Rather than display them the same way every Christmas, he changes things up with different garlands, beads, and branches. It’s a way to get a new look out of decorations he already owns.

Those giant stacked presents in Scott’s house look like they’d be a pain to store, but they’re not. Each box fits inside the next, so the whole display takes up a fraction of the space once Christmas is over.

You can watch the full video and get more tips here:.

At the top of everyone’s mind around the holidays should be safety.

Scott recommends being mindful of fragile decorations, especially if you have young children or large pets. Glass ornaments and other breakable decorations can easily get knocked over, so consider using sturdier pieces in areas where kids and pets spend a lot of time.

The U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC) also recommends looking for a “fire resistant” label when purchasing an artificial Christmas tree and regularly watering live trees to reduce fire risks.

Whether you’re adding a few new touches to your favorite decorations or going all out with a Christmas tree in every room, the most crucial thing is creating a space that feels festive to you.

If maintained properly—and that means having the right tool—wood flooring can hold its finish for years without damage or cracking. Some brooms, for instance, can be too abrasive, whereas mops designed to clean hardwood floors are ideal for these surfaces.
