We put a series of mops for hardwood floors, both cordless and corded, through their paces in a typical home that accumulated dust, dirt, pet hair, and muddy paw prints. We used the mops with their provided cleaners or distilled water, as recommended by the manufacturers.

We noted how easy or difficult the mops were to assemble, and considered the practicality of storing them. Finally, we used each in a controlled test of dried mud and ketchup smeared on hardwood floors and noted how much mess each floor mop left behind.

According to recent reports, when purchasing a mop for wood flooring, think about its ease of use, any cleaning solutions it dispenses, and the price. In addition to the tool itself, factor in the size of the area that needs mopping. Here are some vital considerations to look at when looking at mops for wood floors.

According to recent reports, there are different types of mops available to suit various floor-maintenance preferences: flat mops, string mops, steam mops, and dust mops. Some are used exclusively for dusting floors, while other kinds function as both wet and dry mops.

Recent findings suggest that old-fashioned dunk-in-a-bucket mops require hand-wringing, but there are more convenient, less-messy options today. These mops may feature electric or mechanical components for wringing, as well as either reusable or disposable parts, so look for the type and system that suits your cleaning preference, floor type, and floor size.

The business end of a floor mop is typically either disposable or reusable. Disposable options are convenient for quick touch-ups and smaller floors, while reusable ones often prove more budget-friendly and can tackle larger surfaces.

According to recent reports, both types of mopheads impact sustainability, but in different ways. Reusable mopheads require water and chemicals to launder after use, while disposable versions head straight to the landfill. For larger areas, a reusable, machine-washable mophead is probably more efficient and eco-friendly than using multiple disposable mopheads per cleaning session. Those who prefer a reusable option might consider microfiber mopheads, which will catch and hold dirt and liquids better than materials such as cotton or sponge while reducing the look of scratches and scuffs.

According to Knoll, “Microfiber is the go-to. It’s soft, absorbent, and won’t damage your floors. It also wrings out well, keeping the water usage minimal.” He also added that microfiber mops are “great for picking up dust and fine particles without leaving scratches.”.

According to recent reports, if pushing a manual mop around seems laborious and inefficient, consider an electric model. These products typically have a variety of cleaning modes and processes (including one specifically for wood floors), and may feature the use of steam and/or cleaning solutions. They often come with swiveling heads for easier maneuverability, too.

Sources indicate that electric mops may be corded or cordless—and both types require access to an outlet. Corded mops must be plugged in during use, while the battery charger of cordless models must be plugged in as well. The portability of cordless models tends to appeal to folks who don’t want to be tied down to the length of a cord, typically because they have large areas to clean, and sometimes on different levels.

When stubborn dirt and stains occur, wood floors may require more vigorous cleaning than just dry-mopping, but only with a product specifically formulated for hardwood flooring. While hardwood floors are usually finished and sealed, some versions may be unsealed—it’s vital to avoid using water on unsealed hardwood floors, as well as harsh cleansers on any wood floor. An all-purpose floor cleaner, for instance, may dull or, worse, strip the finish.

Though there are different types of cleaning solutions, those that can be used straight from the container without diluting tend to be safer, since any excess water from mixing a concentrated formula can seep into the wood and damage it. Some mops employ steam to clean and sanitize flooring, which should be safe for sealed hardwood—but to be safe, consult and follow all directions to avoid damage.

Sources indicate that knoll recommends gentle cleaners: “Opt for pH-neutral, hardwood-specific cleaners to prevent damage.” Also, “damp mopping is the way. Ensure the mop is just moist enough to clean without leaving excess water.”.

Recent findings suggest that when it comes to mopping around furniture, under beds/sofas, and into hard-to-reach areas, maneuverability matters. A swivel-head mop is ideal for getting around obstacles. The shape of the mophead (circular, triangular, or rectangular) also impacts how easily it can access corners and tight spots.

Recent findings suggest that mops may also include ergonomic features, some of which affect maneuvering, like telescoping handles to adjust length, and thereby extend reach. A poorly designed handle can also lead to arm and hand fatigue, so users will want to look for a model with a grip that feels good.

Those who still want more information on cleaning hardwood flooring with a quality mop may find it here in the answers to some of the most common questions about this household chore.

Mopping correctly can be a great way to maintain hardwood flooring, but using the wrong cleaning products can actually damage these expensive surfaces. A damp mop is often all that’s required to clean a hardwood floor; if the mop is too wet (with water or cleaning solution), excess liquid can seep into the cracks, causing the wood to warp.

Cleaning a floor starts with removing dust and debris by sweeping, vacuuming, or dry-mopping. For stubborn dirt and stains, use a cleaner designed for the specific floor material, using a “less is more” approach according to the manufacturer’s directions. To mop a floor correctly, dip string or sponge mops in the cleaning fluid, wring it out, and then swab with the damp mop. Use plain water to do a final rinse if desired. Start mopping in a far corner of the room, moving in the direction of the grain on hardwood floors, and work your way to the door. When finished, rinse the mop and let it air dry or wash any reusable pads.

Swiffer’s heavy-duty pads are considered safe for linoleum, vinyl, laminate, and ceramic tile, as well as sealed wood, marble, and stone. They should not be used on unsealed wood floors. As with all floor cleaners, be cautious using any fluid on unfinished, damaged, or especially delicate materials.

Industry observers note that the National Wood Flooring Association recommends a heavy-duty mopping on wood floors monthly with a wood-flooring cleaner. However, it is safe to dry-mop daily or do a light mop on high-traffic areas once a week. For those without children and pets, feel free to give a very light mop on light-traffic areas more often.

Sources indicate that as the executive editor of Product Reviews, Stephanie Cronk has spent years researching and testing products. Cronk has been a pool owner for over 15 years and understands the importance of maintaining a clean pool in the warmer months. Besides her pool experience, Cronk also brings over 12 years of commerce experience to the BobVila.com team, where her focus is on reviewing and testing products in a variety of categories including DIY, home improvement, home appliances, outdoor living, and more.

Imagine cranking up the thermostat on a freezing winter morning to get cozy, only to find that somehow your living room still feels chilly. Maybe there’s a draft coming from the windows, or one area never seems to warm up. Whatever the reason, you might be heating a home that’s letting the warmth escape—and paying through the nose for it.

In a recent development, according to the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency’s ENERGY STAR program, you can save an average of 15% on heating and cooling costs by sealing air leaks and adding insulation where it’s needed. The tricky part? Figuring out exactly where the problems are.

That’s where a thermal imaging camera comes in handy. Instead of guessing which windows need resealing or where insulation might be missing, you can use one to spot temperature differences and take a closer look.

In a recent development, I recently got my hands on both the RISION Magic and Magic Pro thermal cameras and spent time with them around my house. From scanning windows and exterior walls to checking HVAC vents and even tracking my own footprints across the carpet, I was impressed by how much these tiny cameras could reveal.

Better yet, both models are on sale for up to 45% off during Black Friday sales, making now an excellent time to pick one up.

A thermal imaging camera detects infrared radiation emitted by objects and turns this into a visual representation of surface temperatures. Warmer (red, orange) and cooler (blue, purple) areas appear in contrasting colors, allowing you to see temperature differences that you can’t see with your own eyes.

According to recent reports, this opens up some useful possibilities for homeowners. Imagine scanning around a window and spotting a cooler section along the frame. That doesn’t automatically mean there’s an air leak, but it’s a good reason to check the weatherstripping, caulking or surrounding insulation.

You can also use thermal imaging to check on other common household challenges:.

Sources indicate that but remember: thermal imaging isn’t a crystal ball. There can be several reasons for surface temperature differences, and the camera won’t tell you exactly what’s wrong behind a wall. Still, it can help narrow down the places worth checking out before you start ripping off trim or making repairs.

According to recent reports, that’s the appeal of the RISION Magic Series. The camera plugs directly into a compatible USB-C smartphone, tablet or computer, so there’s no need to carry around a bulky device. This thing is about the size of a packet of mints.

I spent a couple of days with the RISION Magic and Magic Pro, and one of my favorite things about these cameras is how little effort it takes to get started.

Sources indicate that there’s no tiresome setup process or annoying account registration. I took the camera out of its box, plugged it into my phone, downloaded the app and started viewing the thermal feed. The whole process took less than two minutes. Considering how many devices require an email address, password and account verification before you can use them, this was a refreshing change.

I was super impressed by the camera’s sensitivity. As I walked around my house, I could actually see the residual warmth of my footprints on the carpet. Plugged-in electronics appeared as warm spots, while my air-conditioning vents stood out in deep blue against the warmer ceiling.

Sources indicate that the app also automatically highlighted particularly hot and cold areas with temperature readouts, making it easy to identify points of interest without constantly examining the entire image. Every now and then, the hotter readouts were difficult to read because the red writing was so close to the red heat source, but a little shift in camera angle normally fixes it.

The RISION Magic is a great entry point if you’re looking to investigate insulation problems, cold spots or other temperature-related concerns around the house. It’s small enough to slip into a pocket and plugs directly into your phone’s USB-C port, so there’s no separate battery or bulky equipment to worry about.

It features a native 160-by-120-pixel thermal sensor, enhanced to 320-by-240 pixels using RISION’s QuadIR processing technology. There’s also a 25Hz refresh rate, which keeps the image reasonably smooth as you move the camera around.

Recent findings suggest that during testing, I liked how clearly the thermal images indicated the framing behind my exterior walls.
